name: fast-alloc
workload: 64-byte allocations: pool, stack and free-list allocators against new/delete, frame workloads.
claimed_speedup: Linux (GCC 14.2.0, Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE): pool allocate/free 2.00 ns vs 6.03 ns new/delete (3.0x); stack allocate/reset 1.99 vs 4.77 ns malloc/free (2.4x); stack 1,000-allocation frame 1205 vs 14385 ns (11.9x); free-list first-fit 4.66 vs 4.67 ns (1.0x); best-fit 0.76x and thread-safe pool 0.60x (slower). The larger ratios are from single-repetition CI runs against weaker system allocators: Windows MSVC pool 14.9x, stack 20.1x/24.0x, free-list 6.7x; macOS pool 4.0x, stack 4.7x/7.0x, free-list 2.2x/1.7x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.0 -O3 -march=native (Linux); Apple Clang 21.0 and MSVC 19.51 Release
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE (Linux); Apple Silicon arm64; Windows CI runner
tradeoffs: Specialised fixed-size pool, stack and free-list allocators for game code, not general-purpose malloc replacements.
caveats: Compares special-purpose pool, stack and free-list arenas, preallocated outside the timed loop, with the general system allocator, a weak baseline; no jemalloc or mimalloc comparison. On Linux the free-list matches malloc (first-fit) or is slower (best-fit, 0.76x), and the thread-safe pool is slower than new/delete on one thread (0.60x). The recorded malloc frame benchmark also allocated and released a pointer array inside the timed loop, which inflates the frame speedups (README says the setup has since changed and fresh results are not comparable). macOS and Windows tables are one CI repetition at 0.1 s minimum time on GitHub-hosted runners with no CPU model. Native CPU optimisation became opt-in on 2026-10-04, after the recorded run. 0 stars; not run.

name: SGCL
baseline: malloc via std::unique_ptr / std::shared_ptr (macOS libmalloc nano zone); also Go and Java ZGC collectors
workload: Per-object allocation cost in ns for 32 B and 256 B objects on 1, 4 and 24 threads, plus binary-trees and a shared-graph workload, compared with unique_ptr, shared_ptr, Go and Java ZGC
claimed_speedup: 32 B allocation 2.8 ns on 1 thread vs unique_ptr 17.1 ns and shared_ptr 16.3 ns (about 6x, derived from page data); 32 B on 4 threads 3.5 vs 17.4 and 16.5 ns; 32 B on 24 threads 11.7 vs 23.2 and 22.6 ns; 256 B on 24 threads is slower than malloc: 71.4 vs 23.5 ns
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG; Go 1.27.1 GOGC=100; OpenJDK 26.0.2 generational ZGC
hardware: Mac Studio Apple M2 Ultra (16 performance + 8 efficiency cores), 64 GB, macOS 26.5
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 concurrent non-moving generational mark-and-sweep GC with its own managed pointer types (tracked_ptr etc.), containers and 15 library modules; programs must adopt sgcl pointer types; conservative stack scanning; tested on Apple Silicon only (Linux and Windows pending).
caveats: The docs deliberately leave the Boehm-Demers-Weiser GC out of the tables, so there is no head-to-head with Boehm GC. The malloc behind unique_ptr/shared_ptr is the macOS nano zone, not glibc, jemalloc or mimalloc (an earlier run with MallocNanoZone=0 made those columns about a quarter slower). C++ columns are from a 4 October 2026 run at -O3; the Go and Java columns are from 19 September 2026, when the C++ side was built at -O2, and were not rerun. Apple Silicon only; no number reproduced on x86-64, Linux or Windows yet. SGCL is slower than unique_ptr for 256 B objects on 24 threads (71.4 vs 23.5 ns), copies a pointer slower than a raw pointer (1.4-1.9 vs 0.6 ns), and uses more memory than unique_ptr in binary-trees (292 vs 134 MB at depth 21). The wall-time wins move destruction to the collector thread, so process CPU time is closer (binary-trees depth 21: 9.41 vs 12.39 s CPU).

Hacker News: WebSearch for concurrent GC library C++ pauseless surfaced the HN thread 'High-performance garbage collection for C++' (news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49695331) and the sgcl repo
WebSearch: 'garbage collector C++ library faster than Boehm GC benchmark github'

corrected_fields.caveats: The docs deliberately leave Boehm-Demers-Weiser GC out of the tables, so there is no head-to-head with Boehm GC; the malloc baseline is macOS nano malloc, not glibc, jemalloc or mimalloc; Go and Java columns were run on 19 Sep 2026 at -O2 C++ build while C++ columns on 4 Oct 2026; no number reproduced on x86-64 or Linux yet; slower than malloc for 256 B objects at 24 threads.

name: v8malloc
workload: Microbenchmarks MB-01 to MB-06: single-thread 8-byte alloc, 8-thread scalability, mixed workload, fragmentation RSS, 256 MiB allocation p99 latency.
claimed_speedup: MB-02 64 B scalability: 4 threads 150.5 M ops/s vs 134.9 glibc, 122.6 tcmalloc, 124.1 jemalloc, 102.6 mimalloc (12% over glibc); 8 threads 296.4 M vs 295.2 glibc, 290.8 tcmalloc, 271.3 jemalloc, 217.5 mimalloc (within noise of glibc and tcmalloc); MB-01 8 B 22 ns/op vs 23 glibc and tcmalloc, 26 jemalloc, 32 mimalloc; MB-06 256 MiB alloc p99 1 us vs 48 glibc, 8 jemalloc, 2 tcmalloc, 160 mimalloc; MB-05 RSS 9.13 MiB, tied with glibc, vs 19.50 tcmalloc and 27.50 jemalloc. Slower on MB-01 16-256 KiB (59-62 vs 24 ns tcmalloc), MB-03 producer/consumer and MB-04 mixed (11.50 vs 22.26 M tcmalloc, 15.42 M glibc).
compiler_and_flags: Clang Release, -flto=auto
hardware: Intel Core Ultra 5 236V (8-core dev container)
tradeoffs: Linux only; early-stage; AddressSanitizer unsupported, ThreadSanitizer experimental.
caveats: Each cell is a single run in an 8-core dev container, and the README itself says to treat single-digit-percent gaps as noise, which covers most of the wins (8-thread MB-02 is 0.4% over glibc, MB-01 small sizes within 1 ns). The clear wins are MB-02 at 4 threads, 256 MiB p99 latency and fragmentation RSS. The README shows it behind tcmalloc and glibc on the mixed workload (11.50 vs 22.26 and 15.42 M ops/s), about 2.5x slower than tcmalloc on 16-256 KiB allocations, and behind mimalloc and glibc on producer/consumer. Clang version not stated; README's make release target uses GCC while the table used clang. Status line says most allocator internals are still being implemented, and this run included a concurrency bug fix in v8m_core_cache_pop_batch (MB-03 SEGV). Linux only. 1 star; not run. [retier] Competitor columns may not measure the stated allocators: benches link v8malloc_static by default (the static archive defines malloc/free), so LD_PRELOAD rows cannot change the allocator and the shared-build 'glibc' row also runs v8malloc (inferred from bench/CMakeLists.txt and bench-compare.sh, not run); the README does not say how competitor columns were built; MB-01/MB-02 call clock_gettime every iteration; most wins are inside the author's own single-run noise band.

name: Boehm-Demers-Weiser GC (bdwgc)
workload: Author's GC benchmark (small-object allocation heavy, C variant), modified to run multiple client threads sharing one heap; elapsed seconds for the GC build versus a malloc/free variant of the same benchmark.
claimed_speedup: docs/scale.md: thread-unsafe collector 9 s vs glibc malloc/free 10.51 s (pthreads not linked), about 1.17x (derived from page data); thread-safe collector (-D GC_THREADS) 10.3 s vs glibc malloc/free 20.90 s (one thread, pthreads linked), about 2.0x (derived from page data); two clients 23.5 s vs 24.55 s, about 1.04x (derived from page data). With -D GC_THREADS -D PARALLEL_MARK -D THREAD_LOCAL_ALLOC the same page lists 1 client 10.45 s (1 marker) / 7.85 s (2 markers) and 2 clients 19.95 s / 12.3 s; against the malloc/free times that is about 2.0x for two clients with two markers (12.3 s vs 24.55 s, derived from page data), though the two-marker runs use the second CPU for marking. The page says the benchmark favors a garbage collector since most objects are small. docs/overview.md says performance is 'typically competitive' with malloc/free, that time and space overhead are 'likely to be only slightly higher' for programs written for malloc/free, that the collector may be faster for very small objects and slower for large ones, and that with thread-local allocation it 'may in some cases significantly outperform' malloc/free; no numbers there.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the baseline comparison (GC built with -D GC_THREADS; later table adds -D PARALLEL_MARK -D THREAD_LOCAL_ALLOC); optimization level unstated.
hardware: Dual-processor Pentium III/500, Linux 2.2.12, ancient GC release from 2000
stars_or_usage: 3.5k stars; packaged in many distributions (Repology badge in README)
tradeoffs: Conservative stack/heap scanning means false retention and no precise object layout; the docs say large-object allocation is slower than malloc and programs usually need more memory; collection pauses unless the incremental mode is used; thread-local allocation and parallel marking are build-time options; GC_MALLOC_ATOMIC and root hints are needed for best speed.
caveats: Only first-party numbers, from a roughly 25-year-old collector release (2000) on a dual Pentium III/500 under Linux 2.2.12 with an old glibc and LinuxThreads; compiler and flags unstated; the author says the workload favors a collector (mostly small objects). The benchmark (GCBench, C variant) is hosted on the author's site (hboehm.info, not reachable from this session) and the multi-client variant used for the table is not published, so the run cannot be reproduced from the repo. The single-thread figure is a modest 1.17x; the 2.0x figure compares a pthreads-linked malloc build, where old glibc/LinuxThreads paid locking cost; the parallel-mark rows use a second CPU for marking while malloc/free runs single-threaded. The project's own docs/overview.md describes performance as typically competitive with malloc/free with slightly higher time and space overhead (citing Detlefs, Dosser and Zorn, 'Memory Allocation Costs in Large C and C++ Programs') and slower for large objects, so the faster claim holds only for small-object-heavy workloads. A third-party 1992 technical report by Zorn (seen only as a search snippet) reports a trivial slowdown versus malloc/free with about twice the memory. License: the LICENSE file is an MIT-style permissive notice (SPDX Boehm-GC, not OSI-listed); gc_allocator.h and extra/msvc_dbg.c carry similar per-file terms, and a few GNU build files carry a modified GPL. The lead URL ivmai/bdwgc is the old home of this repository.

name: ChunkSizedAllocator<N,Sz...> chunked fixed-size-class pool, Packt C++ Memory Management companion code
baseline: glibc/libstdc++ operator new and operator delete (malloc/free)
workload: Book benchmark: 300,000 allocations (100,000 each of 30-, 60- and 100-byte objects) through placement-style operator new(ChunkSizedAllocator&), then destroy and deallocate through std::function, microseconds, one run.
claimed_speedup: Chunked version 12,032 us versus 13,360 us for the standard operator new/delete version, about 90.05% of the standard time (roughly 1.1x, derived from the book's two figures). Numbers are the book's printed figures as relayed in the seed lead; not printed in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Book: online gcc 15 at -O2 (per the seed lead; not in the repo, which only links a wandbox permalink I could not open). libstdc++ inferred from gcc.
tradeoffs: Fixed pools: N blocks per size class (rounded up to powers of two) allocated up front with malloc, allocation falls back to ::operator new when a pool is exhausted or the size does not fit. Freed memory is never reused (deallocate only checks whether the pointer lies in a pool). Deallocation does a linear scan over the size classes. A mutex guards allocate; the lock in deallocate is commented out. new[] and delete[] are left as an exercise.
caveats: First-party book measurement: one run, online gcc 15 at -O2 (per the lead), CPU not stated; the gain is small (about 10%). Benchmark program is chapter10/chunk_sized_allocator.cpp: it prints the two timings but the repo holds no results, compiler line or CPU. The pool's three malloc'd blocks (100,000 slots each of 32, 64 and 128 bytes, about 22 MB) are allocated in the constructor outside the timed region, but their pages are first touched inside the timed chunked run. The std::vector of 300,000 (pointer, std::function) pairs is allocated in each lambda's init-capture before the clock starts and freed after it stops; filling it and the std::function type erasure are timed on both sides. The standard version runs first in the same process. The chunked allocate locks a std::mutex per call while deallocate does nothing; the book itself warns that locking strongly affects the gain and locking in deallocate would likely erase it. No memory reuse (freed slots are never handed out again; when a class fills up, requests fall through to ::operator new), so not like for like with a real allocator. [retier] Enricher: the size-class test is strict (n < sizes[i]), so exact 32/64/128-byte requests skip their class (128-byte objects fall to ::operator new); freed slots are never reused, so after N lifetime allocations per class each call pays the class scan, the mutex and ::operator new and runs slower than the baseline; ::operator delete(p, alloc) skips destructors; std::function and std::pair moves are timed on both sides, diluting the 10%; the file relies on <cstdlib> arriving through other headers. The chapter10 files are unchanged since 2024-08-14 (later commits touch other chapters).

name: mtrebi/memory-allocators (free list allocator; linear, stack and pool allocators)
baseline: malloc/free (libc; the benchmark's CAllocator wraps malloc and free)
workload: Time to Init() the allocator and then perform N allocations (and frees) of fixed or randomly chosen sizes (32 to 4096 bytes, alignment 8) single-threaded, charted against number of operations up to about 1 million for block size 4096; custom linear, stack, pool and free-list allocators versus malloc.
claimed_speedup: README 'Time complexity': 'Malloc is without doubt the worst allocator'; the free list allocator 'is A much better choice than malloc as a general purpose allocator ... It's about three times better than malloc'; linear, stack and pool are faster still but impose restrictions. Exact figures exist only in two chart images (block size 4096, up to about 1M operations; values read off the charts, approximate): with Init() in the timed region malloc about 1500 ms, FREE LIST SEQ about 425 ms, pool about 365 ms, stack about 60 ms, linear about 20 ms; without Init() malloc about 1500 ms, free list about 360 ms, pool about 80 ms, stack and linear about 20 ms. Malloc/free-list ratio about 3.5x with Init and about 4.2x without (derived from page data, chart readings).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. CMakeLists.txt sets only cxx_std_11 and the README build command passes no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so a default build has no optimization flags unless the user adds them.
tradeoffs: Educational implementations: linear (no per-item free), stack (LIFO), pool (single block size) and a first-fit linked-list free-list allocator with minimum-size and alignment constraints; no thread safety, no size classes, no red-black-tree free list (listed as future work).
caveats: First-party, tier C: no hardware, compiler, flags or libc version stated, and the repo's default build (README: plain cmake, no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE; CMakeLists.txt sets only cxx_std_11) has no optimization flags for the custom allocators while libc malloc is prebuilt optimized. The shipped harness cannot reproduce the charts: Benchmark.h defines OPERATIONS as 10 (the `#if 0` branch for the real count is disabled) and main.cpp constructs Benchmark(OPERATIONS), so each round runs 10 operations; the allocator sizes in main.cpp also cannot hold 1M 4096-byte blocks (free list 1e8 bytes, about 24k blocks; pool 16 MiB, 4096 chunks; linear and stack 1e9 bytes, about 244k), so the charts came from an unpublished configuration. The charted free list is 'FREE LIST SEQ' with frees in reverse (LIFO) order, which keeps the free list at one node and makes it behave like a stack; random-order frees would walk the list. The linear and stack allocators never write into the returned memory (the stack keeps its markers in a std::vector), while malloc writes an in-band header into each fresh 4096-byte block, so part of the gap is likely first-touch page faults rather than allocator logic. The timed region includes Init() (one large malloc plus setup), which the README itself says distorts the curves. Correctness bugs in the allocators: FreeListAllocator::FindBest never updates smallestDiff and returns the last node as previousNode; FreeListAllocator::Free never inserts a block whose address is above every free node (it is lost); PoolAllocator::Init mallocs a new buffer each round without freeing the old one. The charts predate later fixes and rewrites ('Stack allcoator bugfix' 2024-05-23, PoolAllocator O(1) initialization 2026-04-02, stack rollback refactor 2026-04-12, empty pool free list fix 2026-09-03), so numbers are on code later changed for correctness. The three-times claim is for the free list only; the faster allocators drop general-purpose semantics. Baseline is plain libc malloc, not jemalloc, tcmalloc or mimalloc. [retier] First-party charts (malloc about 1500 ms vs free list about 360 ms) that cannot be reproduced: the harness is hard-coded to 10 operations, the pool sizes in main.cpp are too small for 1M operations, the default build is unoptimized and the free list is timed only with LIFO frees. The charted test allocates all N blocks (about 4 GB at 1M) before freeing, so malloc pays heap growth and page faults while the linear and stack allocators never touch memory and the old pool Init took its page faults outside the timed region; the 3x gap is likely mostly page faults. Correctness: PoolAllocator::Reset keeps the free list but zeroes the offset (one chunk can go out twice), Init leaks the old buffer, FreeList FindBest returns a wrong previousNode, remainders smaller than the 16-byte header overflow into the next block (issue #4), Free is wrong with nonzero alignment padding (#18), Stack Free ignores ptr. The charts predate the 2024-2026 fixes.

name: SizeBasedArena<T,N> bump arena (Orc Tribe), Packt C++ Memory Management companion code
baseline: glibc/libstdc++ operator new and operator delete (malloc/free)
workload: Book benchmark: allocate then destroy 1,000,000 16-byte Orc objects with class-specific operator new/delete backed by a mutex-guarded bump arena, single thread, std::chrono timing in microseconds, one run.
claimed_speedup: operator new: 23433 us standard library vs 17906 us Meyers-singleton arena vs 17573 us global-singleton arena (arena about 76.4% of the standard time); operator delete: 7943 us standard vs 638 us Meyers-singleton arena (8.03%) vs 0 us global-singleton arena (no-op). Numbers are the book's printed figures as relayed in the seed lead; they are not printed anywhere in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: Book: online gcc 15 at -O2 (per the seed lead; not in the repo, whose files only carry wandbox permalinks that I could not open: wandbox.org ENOTFOUND). libstdc++ inferred from gcc.
tradeoffs: Bump allocation only: freed memory is never reused, delete is a no-op, so memory is reclaimed only when the arena is destroyed. Capacity N*sizeof(T) is malloc'd up front, with no bounds check on exhaustion. A mutex is taken on every allocation. Serves one class (operator new/delete overloads for Orc); operator new[] and delete[] assert false. A SizeBasedArena-safer variant adds static_assert(std::is_final_v<T>) so derived classes cannot be allocated from a too-small slot.
caveats: First-party book measurement: one run on an unnamed online gcc 15 machine (per the lead), CPU not stated; flags and numbers come from the book, not the repo. The repo carries the benchmark programs in chapter10 (carnage-stdlib-version.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-meyers-singleton.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-global-singleton.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-SizeBasedArena.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-SizeBasedArena-safer.cpp) with no printed results or build lines; the record's figures cover only the stdlib, Meyers-singleton and global-singleton variants. Not like for like: the arena never reuses memory, delete does nothing, and the test is allocate-all then free-all, the best case for a bump allocator. The 0 us delete in the global-singleton version means the compiler removed the whole loop (empty deallocate, no static-local guard); the Meyers version's 638 us is mostly the per-call static-local guard check. In the Meyers-singleton version the arena's one-time malloc of 1,000,000 Orc slots (16 MB) runs inside the first timed operator new call, and the arena's pages are first touched in the timed loop on both homemade variants. The std::vector<Orc*> is reserved before timing on all variants. The arena locks a std::mutex per allocation while glibc malloc takes its single-thread fast path. Generic typed-arena speedup over malloc is well known; the evidence is a teaching example. [retier] Enricher: no exhaustion check, so past N lifetime allocations the arena hands out memory beyond its buffer (heap overflow); operator new ignores the requested size, so a derived class overruns its slot (only the -safer variant blocks it); the assert(false) operator new[] applies only to the Tribe variants and has no return (undefined behaviour under NDEBUG), while SizeBasedArena's new[] computes n / sizeof(T) and assumes no array cookie; the delete comparison sets glibc free() against an empty function the optimiser can drop. The chapter10 files are unchanged since 2024-08-14 (later commits touch other chapters).

name: NCCL
baseline: Gloo CPU allreduce_ring (gloo/benchmark/main.cc CPU benchmark, run with -s 2), compared against NCCL on GPUs
workload: Allreduce latency by message size (1 KB to 256 KB on IB RDMA, 1 KB to 2 MB on TCP/IP) between two servers with 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs each, NCCL 2.3.7 versus Gloo commit 1d9e62a running its CPU-buffer allreduce_ring benchmark with -s 2 and 5000 iterations (user-posted GitHub issue; NCCL-side command not shown).
claimed_speedup: gloo issue #158 (Dec 26 2018, user report; NCCL 2.3.7 vs Gloo commit 1d9e62a, 5000 iterations). IB RDMA 100 Gbps: NCCL faster only from 64 KB up: 64 KB 0.13 ms vs 0.155 ms, 128 KB 0.09 ms vs 1.073 ms, 256 KB 0.13 ms vs 20.161 ms (largest size in that table); Gloo faster from 1 KB to 32 KB (1 KB 0.039 ms vs NCCL 0.16 ms; 32 KB 0.088 ms vs 0.15 ms). TCP/IP sockets: NCCL faster from 128 KB up: 128 KB 3.66 ms vs 5.614 ms, 256 KB 6.25 vs 10.980, 512 KB 7.12 vs 20.544, 1 MB 11.91 vs 39.855, 2 MB 20.9 vs 78.237; Gloo faster from 1 KB to 64 KB (1 KB 0.354 ms vs NCCL 1.89 ms; 64 KB 3.813 ms vs 4.02 ms). Largest ratio about 155x at 256 KB on IB, 3.7x at 2 MB on TCP (derived from page data).
hardware: Two Ubuntu servers with 8 V100 GPUs each; 100 Gbps IB RDMA (test 1) or TCP/IP sockets (test 2); CPU model not stated
license: Apache-2.0 for most of the project; some parts keep a BSD-3-Clause license (LICENSE.txt)
tradeoffs: GPU-only collectives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce, broadcast, reduce-scatter, send/recv) over PCIe, NVLink, NVSwitch, InfiniBand verbs and TCP sockets; NVIDIA GPUs and CUDA required; mostly Apache-2.0 with BSD parts (LICENSE.txt), although the README still carries an 'all rights reserved' 2015-2020 notice.
caveats: Weak, apples-to-oranges evidence for such a notable project: the only reachable numbers are one user's report filed against Gloo (reporter: 'gloo has poor performance for large size all-reduce'). The Gloo command is './benchmark ... -s 2 ... allreduce_ring', and allreduce_ring is the CPU-memory algorithm in gloo/benchmark/main.cc (the GPU variants are cuda_allreduce_* in cuda_main.cc), so Gloo ran on host buffers with 2 processes while the NCCL command, buffer placement and rank count are not shown. Gloo's 20.161 ms at 256 KB on IB looks like a Gloo ibverbs pathology rather than a representative baseline. NCCL lost at every size up to 32 KB on IB and up to 64 KB on TCP. Versions are from 2018 (NCCL 2.3.7). The repository README and nccl-tests carry no baseline numbers. Published studies (OSU MVAPICH2-GDR papers, arXiv 1707.09414 and 1810.11112, snippet only since arXiv is blocked) report MVAPICH2-GDR beating NCCL for small messages (up to 17x for 8-byte allreduce per snippet), so NCCL is not uniformly faster than MPI. No CPU model, compiler or flags. Category and domain are a best fit (GPU collective communication has no dedicated category).

name: libpopcnt
baseline: scalar POPCNT loop (unrolled __builtin_popcountll, the std::popcount-style baseline) and the lookup-8 table algorithm; for the 4.2 claim, the library's own earlier scalar POPCNT or Harley-Seal paths
workload: Counting 1 bits in a byte array of 96 bytes to 1 KB using a plain AVX2 popcnt256 loop instead of scalar POPCNT or Harley-Seal (libpopcnt 4.2 ChangeLog entry); the repo's benchmark program otherwise times popcnt() over fixed array sizes (23, 101, 1001, 10001, 16384 bytes in CI).
claimed_speedup: v2.3 README 'Speedup' table (Intel Xeon Platinum 8168, GCC 5.4; speedup over sse-popcount's lookup-8 table algorithm): builtin-popcnt-unrolled 4.75x at 32 B to 7.94x at 4096 B; avx2-harley-seal 1.15x at 32 B, 8.46x at 512 B, 13.66x at 4096 B; avx512-harley-seal 0.35x at 32 B, 15.12x at 1024 B, 25.60x at 4096 B. Against the scalar POPCNT baseline (builtin-popcnt-unrolled) that is about 1.7x for AVX2 and 3.2x for AVX512 at 4096 B, and slower below 256-512 B (derived from page data; libpopcnt picks the fastest algorithm per size). Current ChangeLog 4.2 (2026-07-07): 'Up to 3x faster popcount for medium arrays (96 bytes to 1 KB) using a simple AVX2 popcnt256 loop instead of scalar POPCNT or Harley-Seal' (no numbers or hardware); ChangeLog 2.2: 'Up to 6x faster on old x86 CPUs without POPCNT' (baseline not named). Current README example: 133.5 GB/s for a 16 KB array with the AVX512 algorithm on an AMD EPYC 9R14 (no baseline).
compiler_and_flags: v2.3 README table: GCC 5.4, flags not stated. ChangeLog claims: not stated. README says build with -O3 or -O2 and no -mavx2 needed (runtime CPUID dispatch).
hardware: v2.3 README table: Intel Xeon Platinum 8168. ChangeLog 4.2 claim: not stated. Current README example run: AMD EPYC 9R14 (2023), AVX512 algorithm, 16 KB array.
stars_or_usage: 370 stars; Rust port exists as the simd-popcnt crate
tradeoffs: Header-only; runtime CPUID dispatch (POPCNT, AVX2, AVX512 VPOPCNTDQ, ARM NEON, SVE, PPC64 POPCNTD, portable fallback); no special compiler flags needed; thread-safe. Only counts bits in a byte array (no bitset container).
caveats: First-party evidence only. The library's benchmark program and benchmark.yml CI compare the current code only against its own previous release (job fails if more than 2% slower). The best 'faster than' numbers are an old README table (removed by v3.0, 2024) measured on a Xeon Platinum 8168 with GCC 5.4: the algorithm names and the lookup-8 link point to Wojciech Mula's sse-popcount harness, the program and flags are not named, and the table measures the algorithms rather than necessarily libpopcnt.h itself; the AVX512 path it measured was later replaced (v3.0 swapped AVX512BW Harley-Seal for AVX512 VPOPCNTDQ). Against a plain unrolled POPCNT loop the SIMD paths win only on arrays of a few hundred bytes and up (about 1.7x AVX2 and 3.2x AVX512 at 4 KB, derived) and lose on small arrays, where the library dispatches to scalar POPCNT. The 4.2 'up to 3x' figure compares the new medium-array path with the library's own older paths, with no published numbers in the ChangeLog or the commit (923c433). The AVX2 Harley-Seal algorithm comes from the Mula, Kurz and Lemire paper 'Faster Population Counts using AVX2 Instructions' (peer-reviewed numbers for the algorithm, not for libpopcnt; arXiv blocked here).

name: Cosmopolitan Libc (pthread_mutex_t)
workload: footek_test with USE POSIX: 30 threads each doing 100000 iterations of pthread_mutex_lock, increment a shared counter, pthread_mutex_unlock (heavily contended); wall time of the whole run on Linux 6.8.
claimed_speedup: Comment block in test/libc/thread/footek_test.c, 'with posix', Linux 6.8 AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 7995WX: cosmo 40,965 us real vs glibc 111,560 us real (about 2.7x faster, derived from page data) vs musl 392,765 us real (about 9.6x faster, derived from page data); user time 47,168 us (cosmo) vs 153,985 us (glibc) vs 1,885,558 us (musl); sys time 25,398 us (cosmo) vs 2,988,121 us (glibc) vs 9,667,865 us (musl). Other rows in the same file: FreeBSD cosmo 126,803 us vs freebsd libc 219,073 us (about 1.7x); OpenBSD cosmo 138,619 us vs openbsd libc 385,431 us (about 2.8x); Windows 10 cosmo 156,382 us vs Cygwin 9,334,610 us (not native Windows locks); but Apple M2 Ultra cosmo 65,118 us vs Apple libc 45,443 us (cosmo about 1.4x slower). All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the file (compiler, flags and glibc/musl versions unrecorded).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 7995WX, Linux 6.8 (other rows: Apple M2 Ultra, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Windows 10 test machines)
tradeoffs: Cosmopolitan is a whole libc plus the Actually Portable Executable format, not a drop-in mutex library: using its mutex means building with cosmocc and linking its libc; some platform behavior differs from the host libc; the mutex code is tied to the libc's futex and thread internals.
caveats: Results are first-party comments pasted into a test file, one run each, no compiler, flags or libc versions recorded, so tier C although the test source is public and the CPU is named. Only a single heavily contended 30-thread microbenchmark (100,000 lock/increment/unlock per thread); the timed region also includes creating and joining the 30 threads; it measures aggregate throughput only, not fairness, handoff latency or uncontended lock cost, and says nothing about other libc facilities. The win comes from Cosmo's non-Apple fast path, which calls nsync_mu_lock from third_party/nsync (Google's nsync, Apache-2.0, as modified in Cosmopolitan); on Apple Silicon Cosmo uses ulock instead and the same file shows it slower than Apple's libc. The Windows comparison is against Cygwin, not native SRWLOCK or MSVC locks. name: cppcoro
baseline: concurrencpp (also HPX and libcoro thread-pool runtimes)
workload: Recursive fork-join coroutine benchmarks on 64 worker threads: skynet (100M tasks, forks x10), nqueens (forks up to x14) and fib(39) (forks x2), run with cppcoro's static_thread_pool; matmul(2048) is a tie.
claimed_speedup: Third-party table, absolute times in us: skynet 144907 (cppcoro) vs 12514888 (concurrencpp), 11965484 (HPX), 119686148 (libcoro); nqueens 162773 vs 8000700 / 3452638 / 33347402; fib(39) 269384 vs 20663744 / 10789290 / 238019884. Mean ratio to best 3.67x for cppcoro vs 258.19x concurrencpp, 186.81x HPX, 2513.96x libcoro. Derived from page data: cppcoro is about 86x, 49x and 77x faster than concurrencpp on skynet, nqueens and fib, and about 83x, 21x and 40x faster than HPX. It is slower than tbb (3.25x), taskflow (3.34x), libfork (1.18x) and TooManyCooks (1.32x) on the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.7 Release (CMake preset clang-linux-release, so -O3 -DNDEBUG), -march=native, C++20; code pinned to andreasbuhr/cppcoro commit f05170fbc71aaae06dc31e32812f1caba9525377. Allocator for the cppcoro binaries is not certain: cpp/cppcoro/CMakeLists.txt links mimalloc if found, else jemalloc, and deliberately skips tcmalloc on Linux (falls back to glibc malloc), while the README's machine note says the run was linked against libtcmalloc_minimal.so.4 (which the concurrencpp, HPX and libcoro builds pick first). Baselines pinned in the suite: concurrencpp v.0.1.7, HPX v1.11.0, libcoro commit 44d12235a218a93cf6ce462f67c06a1287901c54.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7742 64-core, 64 worker threads (no SMT), Debian 13 Server, CPU boost enabled, schedutil governor
tradeoffs: Experimental library by its own description; no standard-coroutine-header support in upstream (uses std::experimental style on older compilers), Windows-oriented networking, cmake/cake build. Peak RSS on the fork-join benchmarks is about 134 MB (skynet, nqueens, fib) against 9-14 MB for tbb, taskflow, libfork and TooManyCooks, because the thread-pool runtime allocates a coroutine frame per task.
caveats: Neither the repo README nor any first-party page carries timings: the README makes only qualitative design claims (the static_thread_pool schedule() will not allocate memory in the common case; async_mutex is lock-free). The numbers come from the third-party tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks suite, which measures the maintained fork https://github.com/andreasbuhr/cppcoro (its README lists only build-system, CI and header/namespace-selection changes versus upstream; no performance changes are listed), not lewissbaker/cppcoro itself. The baselines it beats (concurrencpp v.0.1.7, HPX v1.11.0, libcoro) are other coroutine runtimes, not the std::future/std::async baseline from the brief, and no std::async row exists. cppcoro loses to TBB, Taskflow, libfork, TooManyCooks and citor on the fork-join benchmarks (it roughly ties TBB on skynet: 144907 us vs 142887 us) and uses about 10x the memory of TBB or Taskflow (134 MB vs 11-14 MB); in the io_socket_st TCP ping-pong row it is the slowest of four (524717 us vs libcoro 483074 us, Boost.Cobalt 393036 us, TooManyCooks 339340 us). The author of the suite also authors TooManyCooks (a competing runtime). Allocators differ per library: the suite's cppcoro CMake prefers mimalloc, then jemalloc, and otherwise uses glibc malloc on Linux (tcmalloc disabled because it was slower for cppcoro), while the other runtimes take tcmalloc first; the README says the summary machine had tcmalloc_minimal, so which allocator cppcoro actually used is not stated. Each table cell is one process run (warmup plus timed loop) with no repetitions or variance reported. The upstream repo is dormant since 2022-09-02, and the book lead calls it unmaintained. [retier] Enricher: the measured code is the andreasbuhr/cppcoro fork (active through 2026-06-12), which differs from upstream: its static_thread_pool counts sleepers once (notify_intent_to_sleep uses exchange) and it adds a Linux epoll io_service and sockets, so upstream cannot run io_socket_st on Linux. Symmetric transfer is enabled only on Clang 7+ (GCC and MSVC fall back to an atomic handshake, issue #216); the local-queue cap check (m_mask == max_local_queue_size) is unreachable, so the 1 MB cap never applies. name: bluebox
workload: memtier_benchmark with default options (only --hide-histogram and the port given) against a local server on one machine; by the table's ops/sec about 9% SET and 91% GET (18,903.87 of 207,734.88 ops/sec for Redis, a 1:10 ratio), every GET counted as a miss. Redis started with --appendonly no --save ""; Bluebox serving SET/GET/DEL/PING (plus QUIT, DBSIZE, KEYS) on port 9999. The Redis run uses memtier_benchmark from PATH and the Bluebox run uses ./memtier_benchmark, a local binary, so the two runs may have used different client builds.
claimed_speedup: Totals 493,346.12 ops/sec (Bluebox) vs 207,734.88 ops/sec (redis-server), about 2.4x (derived from page data); average latency 0.40524 ms vs 0.96274 ms, p99 0.46300 ms vs 1.87100 ms, p99.9 0.74300 ms vs 3.16700 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile builds with ${CC} -O3 -g ${CFLAGS} src/*.c; compiler name and version not stated, Redis version and build not stated, memtier_benchmark version not stated.
hardware: Linux, AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core (README); kernel, client/server placement and core pinning not stated.
tradeoffs: Demo server for the Neco coroutine library (one coroutine per connection), not a Redis replacement: supports only SET, GET, DEL and PING, no persistence, replication, expiry, pub/sub or data structures beyond a string hashmap. Vendors neco.c (v0.3.2) and tidwall's hashmap.c (v0.8.0) under src/. No pthread use appears in src/bluebox.c, so it runs on one OS thread like default redis-server.
caveats: First-party README numbers from one run with no repetitions or variance (README unchanged since commit fcde463 on 2024-04-15). This is an app-level comparison of a 4-command server against a full-featured Redis, so the gap mostly reflects how much less work Bluebox does per request; it does not isolate Neco from Redis's epoll loop. The thread counts are not equal either: Neco on Linux enables write workers by default (NECO_USEWRITEWORKERS, NECO_MAXIOWORKERS 2, already in the neco.c vendored at the README commit), so Bluebox offloads every socket write to up to 2 extra I/O threads, while redis-server at its default io-threads 1 does all reads and writes on one thread. Both tables show 0.00 hits/sec with all GETs counted as misses, so the GET path measured is the not-found path, not a value copy. The Redis run calls memtier_benchmark from PATH and the Bluebox run calls ./memtier_benchmark (a local build), so the client binaries may differ. Redis version, memtier version, compiler and kernel are unstated. The repo has no LICENSE file (GitHub shows no license); the vendored neco.c and hashmap.c headers say MIT-style and point to a LICENSE file that is absent, and Bluebox's own code is unlicensed, hence usability reference. A transient 2025 commit (25a2011, 'fix neco_main') wrapped SET's body in if (0) and 'enable set' (2190cd7, 2025-05-27) restored it; this postdates the README numbers and HEAD stores keys normally. name: libPhenom
workload: tests/bench/iopipes.c (iopipes.t) event-dispatch benchmark: 1024 AF_UNIX socketpairs (-n 1024), each primed with one byte; every read callback reads the byte and writes one back, so each descriptor stays permanently ready, and the tool counts callbacks dispatched per second over a ~1 s run on one scheduler thread (-c 1). libphenom re-arms with ph_job_set_nbio; the libevent mode (-e) uses the legacy event_init/event_set API with non-persistent EV_READ events re-added via event_add in every callback.
claimed_speedup: Commit 41b6106 'Streamline nbio scheduling a bit' (9 Jun 2013): 'we're a bit faster because we're doing overall less book keeping per event'. Linux, './tests/bench/iopipes.t -n 1024 -c 1': libphenom 366,624 events/s vs libevent ('-e') 264,129 events/s (about 1.39x, derived from page data). OSX: libphenom 505,155 events/s vs libevent 471,385 events/s (about 1.07x, derived from page data). The OSX and Linux boxes are different machines; single core only because that is all the harness can compare against libevent.
hardware: Not stated; the commit says the OSX and Linux numbers came from two different machines. Single core only.
stars_or_usage: 1.7k stars; repository archived 2019-03-09 (README points to folly as the maintained alternative)
tradeoffs: C99 eventing framework (epoll, kqueue, port_create) with its own job scheduler, buffers, hash tables and JSON variants; depends on Concurrency Kit and OpenSSL; any IO thread can service any descriptor (no thread affinity), so more threads add events/s but with a falling per-core rate on the iopipes workload (commit message).
caveats: First-party, single ~1 s runs from one commit message in June 2013; hardware, compiler, flags and libevent version are all unstated, and OSX and Linux numbers came from different machines. The commit added the -e option 'so that it is simpler to gut check against it'. The libevent side of the harness uses the deprecated libevent 1.x API (event_init/event_set) with non-persistent events re-added after every callback rather than EV_PERSIST, which probably costs libevent's epoll backend extra epoll_ctl calls per event, while the same commit makes libphenom track kernel descriptor state to avoid syscalls; libevent is therefore not shown at its fastest. The commit also notes events/s per core drops as scheduler threads are added. Benchmark code (tests/bench/iopipes.c, run-pipes.php, phenom.R) is public, but no charts or later numbers are checked in. Archived 2019-03-09 (README points to folly); last code commit January 2016. The README itself gives no numbers. Category event-loops-io belongs to wave 5, not one of wave 11's categories.

name: Ultimate++ (U++ Core: VectorMap, String, Stream, heap)
baseline: std::map and std::tr1::unordered_map with std::string and std::ifstream (libstdc++ shipped with GCC 4.1.3)
workload: Scan a C source file, collect every C identifier with the lines where it occurs, and sort the identifiers by name, repeated 10000 times with output omitted; U++ VectorMap<String, Vector<int>> and FileIn vs std::map and tr1::unordered_map with std::string and std::ifstream, both with the standard heap and with the U++ allocator.
claimed_speedup: 2007 vsstd page: U++ Core 4.5x to 5.1x vs std::map and tr1::unordered_map (GCC 4.1.3 -O3, Core 2 Duo 2.7 GHz, mixed container, stream and allocator effects); 2020 idmapBench rerun about 2.4x (U++ heap) and 1.8x (malloc) with unequal tokenizing and I/O on the two sides; SortedVectorMap 1.11x slower than std::map.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.1.3 20070929 prerelease (Ubuntu 4.1.2-16ubuntu2) on Ubuntu 7.10 i386 and AMD64, -O3; benchmark defines NDEBUG; the page does not say how the standard-allocator runs were built (the current benchmark package uses the U++ USEMALLOC config flag). 2020 rerun: CLANGx64 Release (Blitz, full debug info), flags not listed.
hardware: Core 2 Duo, 2.7 GHz, 2GB RAM (no CPU model number given)
stars_or_usage: 994 stars on the GitHub mirror; U++ framework in continuous development since the early 2000s
tradeoffs: U++ is a whole framework (its own String, Vector/VectorMap containers with move-only assignment semantics, streams, global operator new/delete overload via the U++ heap, and an IDE/build system, TheIDE), not a drop-in replacement for std containers; adopting the speedup means adopting U++ Core types and its allocator.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party and 2007-vintage (GCC 4.1.3, tr1::unordered_map, Core 2 Duo), and the repo's own 2020 rerun of the updated benchmark (benchmarks/idmapBench/info.txt, Clang x64 on Windows, std::unordered_map) shows the gap shrinking to about 2.4x on the U++ heap and about 1.8x with malloc for both, so the 4.5-5.1x headline is outdated. The measured ratio mixes four effects (container, String vs std::string, U++ FileIn::Get vs per-character std::ifstream::get, and the allocator), so it is not a container-only result; the page itself says the main reason for not using the standard library is not performance. Input files of the 2007 run are not identified (the default input is the benchmark's own main.cpp; the 58 KB file is unnamed), the CPU has no model number, and the allocator switch is not described, so the 2007 run cannot be reproduced exactly. Page only reports GCC rows although the code has an MSVC branch. The rendered ultimatepp.org page was not opened; the repo copy of the topic file was. Category is a judgement call: the benchmark is a word-index container test and fits hash-maps-sets (or allocators) better than filesystems-and-io. name: BaM (Big accelerator Memory)
baseline: CPU-orchestrated GPU storage access (cudaMemcpy over POSIX I/O / GPUDirect Storage)
workload: GPU threads submit NVMe queue requests directly with a software cache, BFS and CC graph analytics, data analytics queries
claimed_speedup: README (ASPLOS'23 abstract): 1.0x (BFS) and 1.49x (CC) end-to-end speedup for graph analytics while reducing hardware cost by up to 21.7x; 5.3x speedup on data-analytics workloads on the same hardware.

name: Direct register access (BSRR) in bare-metal C, Packt Bare-Metal-Embedded-C-Programming companion code
baseline: STM32 HAL GPIO driver call HAL_GPIO_WritePin
workload: Third-party oscilloscope measurement of a PC8 set-then-reset loop on an STM32F072 Discovery (Cortex-M0, 48 MHz): two HAL_GPIO_WritePin calls versus two direct GPIOC->BSRR writes, pulse width read at four optimization levels.
claimed_speedup: BSRR register writes give a shorter pulse than HAL_GPIO_WritePin: 40.80 ns vs 396.0 ns at -O2 and -O3 (9.7x), 61.60 ns vs 418.0 ns at -O1 (6.8x), 61.60 ns vs 896.0 ns at -O0 (14.5x); ratios as printed in the benchmark README table. The book itself gives no timing, only qualitative text and a code-size comparison.
compiler_and_flags: Keil uVision5 with Arm Compiler 6 (AC6), -O0, -O1, -O2 and -O3 compared; other flags not stated (benchmark repo, not the book)
hardware: STM32F072RBT6 (Arm Cortex-M0) on 32F072BDISCOVERY, HCLK 48 MHz from HSE through PLL, 1 flash wait state, PC8 set to high speed; OWON SDS210S oscilloscope (100 MHz, 1 GS/s)
tradeoffs: Direct register writes tie the code to one MCU family and its reference manual, skip the HAL parameter checks and state handling (no error reporting, no clock enabling, no init helpers) and are harder to port than HAL or LL calls. The book's own chapters (Chapter3, Chapter6, Chapter7 and later) are register-level for GPIO, timers, ADC, UART, SPI, I2C, DMA, with its own linker script, startup file and CMSIS headers.
caveats: The numbers are NOT from the book or its repo: the book measures no time (only code size of the same GPIO setup in HAL, LL, C and assembly on STM32F411 at -O0, not in the repo). They come from an unrelated student repo (dotsolvit/stm32f0-gpio-speed-comparison, 0 stars, no LICENSE file in its top-level listing, commits 2026-09-22 to 2026-09-24) measuring the same technique on a different chip (STM32F072 Cortex-M0, not the book's STM32F411 Cortex-M4). Its main.c loop confirms the code (HAL_GPIO_WritePin(GPIOC, GPIO_PIN_8, ...) versus GPIOC->BSRR = GPIO_BSRR_BS_8 / GPIO_BSRR_BR_8, switched by commenting; the committed main.c has the HAL block active) and its method meets tier A, so the tier is capped at B because it measures the technique on another chip rather than the book repo's code. The -O0 row (14.5x) is a debug build; use the -O2/-O3 rows (9.7x). The HAL baseline is fair on parameter checks (stm32f0xx_hal_conf.h leaves USE_FULL_ASSERT off), but the README's claim that HAL is inlined at -O2 is unlikely: the Keil project has LTO off (v6Lto 0) and HAL_GPIO_WritePin lives in a separate driver file, so each HAL write is a real call. The measured pulse width is a toggle-loop artifact: at -O2 and -O3 the BSRR pulse train is non-uniform (grouped pulses, gap every 4 cycles, author attributes it to loop unrolling and flash prefetch, unverified) and ringing is visible below 100 ns. The loop only measures two GPIO writes, not a realistic firmware workload. The book repo's own GPIO driver (Chapter7-GpioInput/Src/gpio.c) writes GPIOA->BSRR |= LED_BS5, a read-modify-write form, not the plain store that was benchmarked. A second independent data point from a tutorial page (VictorTagayun/Basic_DSMPS_Tutorial, NUCLEO-F334R8 at 72 MHz, optimization level not stated): HAL_GPIO_WritePin loop 806 kHz versus GPIOC->BSRR/BRR 2.94 MHz toggle frequency. LL is not compared in either source. Chapter 2 and 6 comparison code (HAL, LL, C, assembly) is not visible in the repo folder listings opened (Chapter1, Chapter2, Chapter7). [retier] Enricher: the README blames the HAL gap on parameter checks and says HAL is inlined at -O2; both are wrong: USE_FULL_ASSERT is off (assert_param is ((void)0U)), LTO is off, and the F0 HAL_GPIO_WritePin is a branch plus one BSRR/BRR store called out of line, so the measured gap is call overhead only. Each row is a hand-edited build (the committed main.c has the HAL block on), with no build logs or disassembly. The benchmark repo has no licence: cite the numbers, do not copy its code. The book's own code uses BSRR |= (a needless read), ODR ^= (not interrupt-safe) and empty for-loop delays.

name: STM32 Low Layer (LL) driver library
workload: Third-party GPIO pin toggle loop at 72 MHz: HAL_GPIO_WritePin set/reset versus LL_GPIO_SetOutputPin/LL_GPIO_ResetOutputPin versus HAL_GPIO_TogglePin versus LL_GPIO_TogglePin versus direct BSRR/BRR register writes, toggle frequency measured on PC9 of a NUCLEO-F334R8 (tutorial) and on PA8 in the linked STM32F334_HAL_LL_REG_GPIO project (each variant commented in or out of one while loop).
claimed_speedup: No valid numeric win: the tutorial's LL set/reset rate (1.09 MHz) against HAL_GPIO_WritePin (806 kHz), about 1.35x (derived from page data), comes from an unoptimised build in which the static inline LL functions were not inlined; optimised, LL compiles to the same single store as direct register access. Toggle rates were equal (625 kHz).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. The linked .ioc names STM32CubeIDE as the toolchain (STM32Cube FW_F3 V1.10.0, HAL full assert off); the optimization level is not given and no IDE build configuration is in the repo.
hardware: Tutorial: NUCLEO-F334R8 (STM32F334R8, Cortex-M4F), 8 MHz external clock with PLLMUL 9, 72 MHz system clock. Linked repo's .ioc targets STM32F334C8Tx with a 72 MHz PLL clock.
stars_or_usage: 209 stars, 76 forks (STM32F4 HAL/LL driver repository); the STM32Cube MCU component hal_driver for the STM32F4 series
tradeoffs: LL is closer to the registers than HAL: no handle structures, no state machine, little or no parameter validation and no timeout or error handling in the register-level calls, so peripheral setup order, clock enabling and error paths are the caller's job. LL is not offered for every peripheral (ST's driver manuals reportedly say it is not provided where optimized access is not a key feature, USB for example; search snippet only) and code is less portable across STM32 families than HAL.
caveats: The speed numbers are third-party, from a hobby tutorial (Basic_DSMPS_Tutorial, 5 stars) and its linked test repo, not a controlled study, and from the STM32F3 family (STM32F334 with STM32Cube FW_F3), not the F4 driver repo this record points at; the LL GPIO API is shared across families. Compiler optimization level is not stated anywhere (the .ioc says STM32CubeIDE, HAL assert off, PA8 high speed; no build config committed). The two sources disagree on the plain register loop (2.94 MHz on PC9 versus 5.54-6.00 MHz on PA8 for the same BSRR/BRR writes), and the linked repo's comments show the same register code at 5.54 MHz in a HAL-generated project and 6.00 MHz in an LL-generated one, so build settings differed between runs and a low-optimization (Debug) build is plausible for the tutorial figures. The gain is only for separate set/reset calls (about 1.35x); TogglePin shows no LL gain, and direct register writes beat both APIs by 2.7x to 5x. ST's release notes describe the LL drivers as 'optimized and one shot services' without numbers; the repository README makes no speed or footprint claim. Code-size evidence exists only as forum snippets not opened (community.st.com and eevblog.com unreachable): a GPIO plus LPUART build reportedly 10128 bytes with HAL versus 5848 bytes with LL, chip and flags unstated. [retier] Enricher: the same direct-register code ran at 5.54 vs 6.00 MHz across the two projects, showing build drift; measured on STM32F3 parts (F334R8, F334C8), not the F4 driver; the tutorial has no licence.
found_via: seed-record pass from https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32f4xx_hal_driver; third-party timing found via WebSearch 'stm32 HAL versus LL performance test DWT cycle count results table' which surfaced https://github.com/VictorTagayun/Basic_DSMPS_Tutorial

verification.tier_reason: Third-party hobby tutorial (5-star repo) whose toggle loop code is public (linked VictorTagayun/STM32F334_HAL_LL_REG_GPIO Src/main.c) and whose board and clock are stated, but the optimization flags are not, and it is not a well-known independent suite, so C rather than A or B.
verification.notes: Numbers on the tutorial page match the record; linked repo main.c gives a second, consistent set (LL set/reset about 1.34x over HAL_GPIO_WritePin, toggle equal). Category filesystems-and-io looks wrong for an MCU GPIO driver layer (closer to an embedded/runtime category); consider a category override, and consider pointing repo_url at STMicroelectronics/stm32f3xx_hal_driver since the measurement used F3 parts (not checked here).

retier.reason: C to D: LL_GPIO_SetOutputPin/ResetOutputPin are static inline single BSRR (F3: BRR) stores, the same instruction as the direct-register loop, yet LL measured 1.09/1.18 MHz against 2.94/5.54-6.00 MHz for the register loop, so the LL calls were not inlined: an unoptimised build at an unstated -O level. The only numeric win (about 1.35x over HAL) is a Debug-build artifact, not LL speed (-O0 downgrade precedent; no valid measurement).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: LL_GPIO_SetOutputPin/ResetOutputPin 1.09 MHz vs HAL_GPIO_WritePin set/reset 806 kHz (about 1.35x, derived from page data); HAL_GPIO_TogglePin and LL_GPIO_TogglePin both 625 kHz (no gain); direct GPIOC->BSRR/BRR 2.94 MHz.
corrected_fields.workload: Third-party GPIO pin toggle loop on a NUCLEO-F334R8 (72 MHz): HAL_GPIO_WritePin set/reset versus LL_GPIO_SetOutputPin/LL_GPIO_ResetOutputPin versus HAL_GPIO_TogglePin versus LL_GPIO_TogglePin versus direct GPIOC->BSRR/BRR, measured toggle frequency on PC9.
corrected_fields.hardware: NUCLEO-F334R8 (STM32F334R8, Cortex-M4), 8 MHz external input with PLLMUL 9, system clock up to 72 MHz
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 209 stars (STM32F4 HAL/LL driver repository); shipped beside HAL in the STM32Cube MCU packages
corrected_fields.caveats: The speed numbers are third-party, from a different family (STM32F334, not the F4 driver repo this record points at; the LL API is shared across families) and from a tutorial page, not a controlled study. The compiler and optimization level are not stated: a linked repo (VictorTagayun/STM32F334_HAL_LL_REG_GPIO) holds the toggle main.c with each variant commented in or out and an .ioc file (STM32CubeIDE, HAL assert off, PA8 high speed), but its README has no results or flags. HAL overhead varies about 2x between -O0 and -O1 in another STM32F0 test, so a default Debug build could inflate the gap. The toggle-pin variants show no LL gain. ST's own claim (LL is leaner and faster than HAL) has no numbers on the F4 driver repository page I opened (no benchmark or footprint data seen; Release_Notes.html was not opened). Code-size evidence exists only as forum snippets that I could not open (community.st.com and eevblog.com are ENOTFOUND here): a post titled 'Is HAL driver Require more space compared to LL' reportedly shows a GPIO plus LPUART build of 10128 bytes with HAL versus 5848 bytes with LL, chip and flags unstated (snippet only), and an EEVblog comment reports about 6K to 2K for a basic build (snippet only).

name: uring-sync
baseline: cp -r (read/write syscalls); rsync over SSH for network
workload: Local copy of 100K x 100KB and 100K x 4KB files on NVMe, cold cache; and 9.7GB laptop-to-GCP transfer with kTLS.
claimed_speedup: 4.2x faster than cp -r (5.4s vs 22.7s, 100K x 100KB); 1.5x on 100K x 4KB (5.14s vs 7.67s); 3.2x on GCP pd-standard (19s vs 60s); 58% faster than rsync over network (165s vs 390s, 9.7GB).
hardware: Local NVMe on an unnamed Ubuntu laptop (CPU model not stated); GCP pd-standard VM
tradeoffs: Linux-only (io_uring, splice, kTLS need recent kernels); copy-tool, not a general library; single worker with deep queue design.
caveats: First-party numbers, apparently single runs; CPU model and compiler flags not stated; baseline is cp -r, not a raw read/write or io_uring baseline; speedup depends on many-small-file workloads (only 1.5x on 100K x 4KB locally). Network rsync baseline was run as rsync -az (compression on, SSH encryption) against uring-sync plaintext-protocol with kTLS AES-128-GCM; on 10K x 6KB (60MB) uring-sync kTLS was slower than rsync (2.98s vs 2.63s), and 34% faster at 589MB. kTLS + splice mode measured 2.9x slower than read/send in its own docs. Pre-shared-secret protocol, not a drop-in rsync replacement (no delta transfer).

name: libuv io_uring file backend
workload: Async read, write, fsync, fdatasync, stat via io_uring instead of the threadpool (libuv 1.45+).
claimed_speedup: Commit message (#3952): 'Performance looks great; an 8x increase in throughput has been observed.' No methodology given.
tradeoffs: Linux only, kernel dependent, falls back to threadpool; some ops (access) have no io_uring path.
caveats: No workload, hardware or method is given; the baseline is libuv's own threadpool, not POSIX I/O. Per search results, libuv 1.49 made io_uring opt-in (UV_USE_IO_URING=1) after kernel and security problems (SQPOLL); in 1.50 io_uring is used for epoll batching, and the env var now affects only sqpoll. Default builds may therefore not use the io_uring file path at all. Node.js also patched io_uring off by default in its bundled libuv. Docs are CC-BY-4.0; code is MIT.

name: loguru
workload: Google Benchmark, one synchronous formatted INFO log call per iteration written to a log file with stderr output disabled: a message struct of four integers (u64, i64, u32, i32) and a 128-byte char string, cycling through pre-generated random messages. loguru uses printf-style LOG_F with its default unbuffered mode (g_flush_interval_ms = 0, flush per line); glog uses stream LOG(INFO) << with a custom prefix function and FLAGS_logbufsecs=0. Two scenarios: iterations:2000 x 5 repetitions at 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 threads, and min_time 3 s at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. loguru v2.1.0 vs glog v0.6.0; report run 2025-02-21.
claimed_speedup: All ratios derived from page data (Time column, loguru vs glog). Iterations scenario (mean of 5): 1 thread 2392 vs 4324 ns (1.81x faster); 3 threads 4383 vs 3734 ns (glog 1.17x faster); 6 threads 4134 vs 5022 ns (1.21x); 12 threads 5398 vs 5927 ns (1.10x); 24 threads 4264 vs 5932 ns (1.39x). min_time 3 s scenario: 1 thread 2357 vs 4378 ns (1.86x); 2 threads 3265 vs 3674 ns (1.13x); 4 threads 4029 vs 4196 ns (1.04x); 8 threads 3434 vs 5357 ns (1.56x). CPU-time column favours loguru at every thread count (e.g. 24 threads 8284 vs 19366 ns). The project's own README claims 25%-75% faster than GLOG on a MacBook Pro (Clang), about the same on a Linux desktop (GCC) in unbuffered mode, and about twice as fast with ~100 ms buffered flushing.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 14.2.1 20240910, glibc 2.40; build.sh passes -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON (CMake's Release default for GCC is -O3 -DNDEBUG; not echoed in the report); CMakeLists.txt adds -Wall -Wextra and C++17; Google Benchmark v1.8.3
hardware: Intel i7-10710U (12 threads), ThinkPad X1 Carbon 7th, Arch Linux kernel 6.11.9, frequency pinned to 3.2 GHz with scripts/set_cpu_freq.sh, 15659 MiB RAM (report dated 2025-02-21)
tradeoffs: Single loguru.hpp/loguru.cpp pair with no #includes in the header (README: about 10% faster compilation than including glog in a medium project). printf-style by default, optional streams (LOGURU_WITH_STREAMS) and fmtlib. In the independent run neither logger scales with thread count and the lead over glog shrinks or flips under contention. Public-domain dedication carries no patent grant.
caveats: Benchmark is a third-party logger shootout (MuggleWei/cc_log_benchmark, 34 stars), not the loguru author's. The baseline glog v0.6.0 is old and google/glog itself was archived on 2025-06-30 (README points to ng-log and Abseil logging); loguru is v2.1.0 while the repo's latest commit bumps the version to 2.2.0. Per-line work is not identical: glog formats with iostreams and a custom prefix function and is built as a shared library (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON), while the loguru benchmark #includes loguru.cpp into the same translation unit and prints its default prefix with uptime and thread name. The Time column for multithreaded runs is (sum of per-thread time / threads) / total calls, not single-call latency; glog wins at 3 threads (4383 vs 3734 ns) and the 4-thread min_time margin is only 1.04x. Single laptop, one run per configuration; stddev only for the iterations rows. The shootout's own conclusions single out fmtlog, haclog, Nanolog and quill as the faster libraries, not loguru. The project's own bench dirs (loguru_bench, glog_bench) are public but its README numbers give no CPU model, compiler version or glog version. Unlicense: public-domain dedication, no patent grant.

name: Boost.Log
baseline: std::fstream with std::flush after every line (also stdio fprintf+fflush and g3log 1.3.2)
workload: Third-party logging benchmark by the author of the reckless logger: per-call latency for periodic calls, call bursts and calls interleaved with heavy disk I/O, plus total overhead of logging about one million lines from a multithreaded Mandelbrot computation, all with a synchronous Boost.Log text file sink writing to log.txt.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, and slower than the named baseline in most scenarios. Lower overhead than std::fstream only in multithreaded Mandelbrot and the disk-I/O scenario: 4 threads 13.17 vs fstream 15.66 and stdio 15.03 (about 1.19x lower than fstream, derived from page data), 8 threads 1.82 vs fstream 4.62 and stdio 3.70 (about 2.5x lower, derived from page data), disk I/O 46.03 vs fstream 5719.93 relative call latency (about 124x, derived from page data; fstream flushes every line and hits multi-second kernel stalls while the Boost.Log adapter does not flush). Beats g3log 1.3.2 in periodic calls (67.42 vs 78.19) and call bursts (3.84 vs 4.20). Slower than std::fstream, stdio and spdlog in periodic calls (67.42 vs 41.32, 43.77, 40.85), call bursts (3.84 vs 2.36, 2.55, 1.93) and 1-thread Mandelbrot (15.21 vs 10.73, 12.21, 9.21; slowest of all). All values are relative to reckless (1.00).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0 and Boost 1.65.0 per the page; the optimisation flags of the published run are not stated (the benchmark build rules use -O3 when CONFIG_DEBUG is not 'yes', while tup.config.template defaults to CONFIG_DEBUG=yes).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X 3.7 GHz, 8 cores, SMT off; Samsung 970 EVO 1TB NVMe SSD; WD Red 3TB HDD on a Synology DS216j for the disk-I/O scenario; 32 GiB RAM; Linux 4.14.65
stars_or_usage: 212 stars; part of the Boost C++ Libraries
tradeoffs: Large, highly modular and extensible library (sources, filters, formatters, many sink backends) with a heavy abstraction level and Boost dependencies. The library's own README and docs (rationale, intro) state performance as a goal but publish no numbers; repo test/performance holds only internal timing programs (record_emission.cpp, dump.cpp) with no external baseline.
caveats: Boost.Log is not claimed to be fast by its authors, and the numbers come from a competitor's benchmark (reckless) in which Boost.Log is slower than reckless, spdlog and often plain stdio and std::fstream. Its only wins against std::fstream (4- and 8-thread Mandelbrot, disk I/O) are tilted by configuration: the reckless adapter (benchmarks/boost_log.hpp) uses add_file_log without keywords::auto_flush, so Boost.Log writes through a buffer and does not flush per record, while the fstream adapter ends every line with std::endl or std::flush and the stdio adapter calls fflush; the 124x disk-I/O ratio is driven by multi-second synchronous flush stalls in fstream, which a buffered ofstream would avoid. Results are from Boost 1.65.0 and gcc 7.3.0 (about 2018), the flags of the published run are not stated (tup.config.template defaults to CONFIG_DEBUG=yes, which Tuprules.lua builds at -O0; release is -O3), and the page gives charts plus relative-time tables with IQR only. Other third-party shootouts show Boost.Log slower than the incumbents they list: NanoLog README latency table (Boost 1.55 1764 ns vs glog 1198 ns vs spdlog 214 ns, static string, 50th percentile) and an older spdlog README table (boost log 1.54 4.169 s vs glog 1.066 s vs spdlog 0.302 s for 1M lines, single thread; snippet only, page not opened, row no longer in the current README). Boost.org documentation was not reachable from this environment.

name: Easylogging++
workload: Time to write 1,000,000 short text lines ('message #N: This is some text for your pleasure') to a log file, split across 1, 10 or 100 threads that share an atomic counter; best of 3 runs; Easylogging++ file output with default logger, format '[%datetime]: %msg', large flush threshold, against glog LOG(INFO) to a log directory.
claimed_speedup: From the spdlog v0.16.3 README benchmark table (seconds, lower is better): 1 thread 0.975s (Easylogging++) vs 1.066s (glog), about 1.09x faster (derived from page data); 10 threads 2.857s vs 3.032s, about 1.06x faster (derived from page data); 100 threads 4.512s vs 1.139s, i.e. Easylogging++ about 4.0x slower than glog (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: bench/Makefile in gabime/spdlog v0.16.3: CXX ?= g++ (version not stated), -march=native -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -std=c++11 -pthread -O3 -flto -DNDEBUG; glog linked with -lglog (version not stated); Easylogging++ included from a local checkout (-I../../easylogging/src/) with config bench/easyl.conf (FORMAT '[%datetime]: %msg', TO_FILE true, TO_STANDARD_OUTPUT false, PERFORMANCE_TRACKING false, MAX_LOG_FILE_SIZE 10485760, Log_Flush_Threshold 10485760). _ELPP_THREAD_SAFE is defined only in easylogging-bench-mt.cpp, not in the single-thread easylogging-bench.cpp. The programs contain no timer, so whole-process wall time was presumably measured externally; no run script is in the bench directory.
hardware: Ubuntu 64 bit, Intel i7-4770 CPU @ 3.40GHz
tradeoffs: Single-header, many features (custom sinks, performance tracking, hierarchical loggers, macros that define global state, _INITIALIZE_EASYLOGGINGPP). Repo archived read-only on 2025-07-06; its own README now recommends spdlog for new projects. Heavy macro and global-state design.
caveats: Evidence is a competitor's benchmark (spdlog author) from about 2015-2016, with Easylogging++ and glog versions and the g++ version unstated and the Makefile pointing at a local checkout (-I../../easylogging/src/); the bench sources use the leading-underscore macros _INITIALIZE_EASYLOGGINGPP and _ELPP_THREAD_SAFE, which current Easylogging++ spells without the underscore, so an old release was measured. Mixed result: Easylogging++ wins by 6-9% at 1 and 10 threads but loses about 4x at 100 threads. Asymmetric configuration: Easylogging++ is set to a short '[%datetime]: %msg' line, while glog writes its full default prefix (severity, date, microsecond time, thread id, file:line) on every line and no FLAGS_log_prefix change is made, so glog formats and writes more bytes per message; the single-thread Easylogging++ binary is built without _ELPP_THREAD_SAFE (no locking) while glog always takes its mutex. The 6-9% wins are small enough that these differences can account for them. The programs contain no timer, so the timed region is the whole process including logger setup, and the measurement method is not in the repo. Both libraries write to file with mostly default buffering. The project's own README says only 'Extremely fast' with no numbers, and its maintainer notes third-party benchmarks of limited setups (links g3log issue #73). That issue (https://github.com/KjellKod/g3log/issues/73, null sink, unstated units, no compiler or CPU) shows Easylogging++ 410,725 vs glog 402,970 for 1 thread string, but glog ahead at 4 threads (196,734 vs 127,895 without the option); this is directional and not used for the tier. spdlog itself is about 3x faster than either in the same table. The repository was archived by its owner on 2025-07-06 and its README recommends spdlog for new projects. [retier] Enricher: the earlier note that both libraries write with mostly default buffering is wrong for Easylogging++: by default it flushes after every entry and echoes every line to stdout, and the bench turned both off (Log_Flush_Threshold 10,485,760 entries, so no flush during the run; TO_STANDARD_OUTPUT false), so a tuned configuration was measured against a default glog. The _ELPP_ macros show v9.75 or older was measured (v9.80 drops the underscore). glog at 100 threads (1.139 s) beat glog at 10 threads (3.032 s), an unexplained inversion with no run script or repeat data. Open, unanswered issues include a disk-full rolling deadlock (#744) and a multi-threaded performance-tracking crash (#790).

claimed_speedup: Regex parsing: Fluent Bit 3.2.7 20.5 MiB/s vs Fluentd 4.5.2-1 2.6 MiB/s (about 7.9x, derived from page data) and Logstash 8.17.3 4.6 MiB/s (about 4.5x, derived from page data). File to TCP, multi-file (older versions: Fluent Bit 1.1.0, Fluentd 3.3.0-1, Logstash 7.0.1): 35 MiB/s vs 26.1 MiB/s (about 1.3x, derived from page data) and 3.1 MiB/s (about 11x, derived from page data); peak memory there 370.3 MiB vs 890.6 MiB and 763.7 MiB.
hardware: AWS EC2: subject c5.large (2 vCPU), five c5.large producers and a c5d.xlarge consumer for the regex case (cases/regex_parsing_performance/configurations/default/terraform.tfvars); subject c5.large and consumer c5.xlarge for file-to-TCP multi_file (cases/file_to_tcp_performance/configurations/multi_file/terraform.tfvars). stars_or_usage: 8.2k stars; CNCF graduated (Fluentd ecosystem); README says it is deployed over 10 million times daily and has passed 15 billion downloads
tradeoffs: In the regex test Fluent Bit peaked at 584.5 MiB of memory vs 246.1 MiB for Fluentd (743.8 MiB for Logstash), so the throughput win costs memory there; in the file-to-TCP case it used less memory than both. Written in C with plugins in C, Lua filters and Go outputs (per README).
caveats: Measured by the Vector project (a competing log router) in its public test harness, not by Fluent Bit's authors; results are single runs without variance, and the same tables show Vector beating Fluent Bit on file-to-TCP (76.7 vs 35 MiB/s) and TCP-to-TCP. Instance types are public in the cases' configurations/*/terraform.tfvars (c5.large subject), but the exact CPU model is not given and packages are prebuilt, so no compiler or flags exist, hence not tier A. Subject configs are public (cases/regex_parsing_performance/ansible/config_files): every tool runs its default single process/worker with the same regex; Fluent Bit and Fluentd both peak at about 50% CPU user on the 2-vCPU subject (one core), Logstash uses grok and reaches 90.5%. In the regex case Fluent Bit used more memory than Fluentd (584.5 MiB vs 246.1 MiB peak), and Fluentd forwards with its msgpack forward protocol while Fluent Bit sends json_lines over TCP. Versions differ per case: the file-to-TCP table is from 2019 releases, the regex table was refreshed in the harness' 2026 refresh commit (#101, 2026-06-18); the Fluentd version label (4.5.2-1) looks like a td-agent package version, not the Fluentd core version (not checked against the harness bootstrap). The harness README warns it is under construction and not fully validated against recent versions. Fluent Bit's own documentation claim of roughly 650 KB idle memory vs about 40 MB for Fluentd (seen only as a search-result paraphrase) could not be opened because docs.fluentbit.io did not resolve; no Fluent Bit-run benchmark was reachable. The harness' TCP-to-HTTP and TCP-to-blackhole case pages were not opened; their Fluent Bit vs Fluentd figures (19.6 vs <1 MiB/s and 64.4 vs 27.7 MiB/s) were seen only in a copy of Vector's README performance table at https://github.com/appsignal/vector, which gives no hardware or versions. [retier] Enricher: 'IO Thrpt' is the subject's net_recv_avg (ingest) per bin/compare; filters run at ingest, so parse speed is real but delivery is unmeasured. The harness config sets no Mem_Buf_Limit, so buffering is unbounded (matching the 584.5 MiB peak); sent/received 1.6 GiB/1.2 GiB against Vector's 2 GiB/804.8 MiB suggests a backlog at the end of the run (derived from page data, unconfirmed). compare averages all runs of the latest version (run count not shown), not single runs. The 3.2.x line is end of life; critical advisories GHSA-5rjf-prwh-pp7q (2024) and GHSA-jrp8-r9hx-gf73 (2026).

name: G3log
baseline: Boost.Log (asynchronous_sink with text_ostream_backend, auto_flush off) in the Quill logger_benchmarks latency tables; also std::fstream with std::flush after every line and Boost.Log in the reckless doc/performance.md Disk I/O scenario (g3log is not faster than stdio fprintf+fflush there)
workload: Quill logger_benchmarks call-site latency: each observation is the average of 20 log calls made in a tight loop ('Logging int: {}, int: {}, double: {}' and a variant with a std::string over 35 characters), about 2 ms between observations, 1 and 4 caller threads, backend thread pinned to CPU 5; g3log LOG(INFO) to its default file logger vs Boost.Log BOOST_LOG_SEV to an asynchronous text sink. reckless Disk I/O: average latency of 2048 log calls, each interleaved in the same thread with writing 32 MiB to a new file (64 GiB over 2048 files), every library flushing to the OS per call; plus Mandelbrot total-overhead rows with 4 and 8 worker threads.
claimed_speedup: 1 thread: 2.9-3.2x lower latency than Boost.Log (derived from page data); 4-thread Boost.Log rows invalid (data race in the harness); g3log second-slowest in the table and 3-4x slower than spdlog.
compiler_and_flags: Quill tables: GCC 14.2, CMake Release with CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS -m64 -march=x86-64-v3 (logger_benchmarks CMakeLists.txt), C++20, static libraries, g3log built from source at commit 8217b08 per vendor_manifest.json (the README does not say which g3log commit produced the table). reckless doc: gcc 7.3.0, -O3 -ggdb3 -std=c++11 from Tuprules.lua; g3log 1.3.2 library build flags not stated.
hardware: Quill tables: Intel Core i5-12600 (12th Gen) @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, benchmark-tuned kernel (isolcpus=1-5, nohz_full, mitigations=off). reckless doc: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X 3.7 GHz, 8 cores, SMT off, 32 GiB RAM, Samsung 970 EVO SSD, Linux 4.14.65; its Disk I/O scenario wrote to a WD Red WD30EFRX 3 TB mechanical disk in a Synology DS216j NAS.
tradeoffs: Asynchronous logger: log calls format the message at the call site and push it to a queue serviced by a background sink thread, with dynamic sinks and crash-safe flush on fatal signals. Messages queued at a crash are written by the signal handler; throughput is bounded by the single background thread. Unlicense/public domain gives no patent grant.
caveats: g3log beats only the slowest or synchronous baselines. In the Quill tables it is second-slowest, ahead of Boost.Log only, and roughly 3-4x slower than spdlog at every percentile; it is absent from Quill's complex-type and throughput tables. Both benchmark pages are written by authors of competing libraries (Quill, reckless). In the reckless doc the 186x figure is std::fstream with std::flush blocking behind a 64 GiB write storm to a NAS mechanical disk, and g3log is slower than plain stdio fprintf+fflush in that same table; across the other reckless scenarios g3log is slow: periodic calls 78.19 vs stdio 43.77, fstream 41.32, spdlog 40.85, boost_log 67.42 (slowest listed), call burst 4.20 vs stdio 2.55, fstream 2.36, boost_log 3.84, Mandelbrot single thread 13.40 vs stdio 12.21, fstream 10.73. The reckless g3log wrapper benchmarks/g3log.hpp is not in the repo (404 at master), so those rows cannot be rebuilt from public code, and they use g3log 1.3.2 with gcc 7.3.0. The README's ~2 us figure is first-party on 2010 hardware with no baseline; the author's worst-case-latency blog post was not reachable. Unlicense public-domain dedication: no patent grant. [retier] Call site about 1 us; unbounded queue with no backpressure; one thread per sink; fatal handler not async-signal-safe, SIGTERM treated as fatal; messages before initializeLogging dropped; reckless 186x over fstream is a NAS write storm; Unlicense, no patent grant.

name: P7Baical (libP7)
baseline: printf() to console and vsprintf() to a memory buffer (stdio analog of std::cerr); not a logging library
workload: Speed test in the P7 manual: messages per second for printing a simple formatted string to a memory buffer, to the console, and as a P7 trace message (saved to a file) on an Intel i7-870.
claimed_speedup: Figure on page 11 of Documentation/P7.pdf (Intel i7-870, 16.03.2015, sink = file): 'Printing speed: P7 trace: 5 210 000 per sec; Buffer: 688 000 per sec; Console: 10 000 per sec' (about 7.6x the buffer print and 520x the console print, derived from page data). Text on page 10: i7-870 sends 50 000 traces per second at 0.5% CPU, max ~3.3 million per second to the network server.
hardware: Intel i7-870 (manual figure dated 16.03.2015); manual also lists Intel E8400 and ARM 926EJ numbers for P7 alone
stars_or_usage: 26 stars (CMake port repo); upstream distribution at baical.net
tradeoffs: Binary trace format needs the Baical server/viewer (or P7 file reader) to read logs; asynchronous delivery through a client-side buffer pool; C, C++, C# and Python clients; LGPL-3.0-or-later; no dependencies.
caveats: No head-to-head against any logging library (the manual never names spdlog, glog or log4cplus); the only baselines are printf and vsprintf. The P7 side is a call-site enqueue into a ring buffer drained by a background thread: in Tests/Speed/Speed.cpp the timer stops before the client is released, so delivery to the file is not timed, and it is not comparable to a synchronous console print. The buffer case formats 6 arguments with vsprintf ('[%s][%s][%d][%d][%d] ... iteration is %d') while the P7 trace call passes 1 argument (P7 captures file, function, line, thread and processor as binary metadata and defers formatting); the console case calls printf with the already formatted buffer as the format string, so it prints the previous line unformatted and without a newline, i.e. it times raw terminal output. The shipped Speed.cpp prints its results as text, while the page-11 figure plots 'To P7trace/To Buffer/To Console' counters (Count 1000) in the Baical viewer and quotes its Max column, so the 2015 screenshot came from a different build of the test. The page-10 figures (50 000 traces/s at 0.5% CPU, ~3.3 million/s max on i7-870) were measured with /P7.Sink=Baical over loopback, not to file. Compiler and flags are unstated; numbers are first-party and from 2015. The manual and Speed.cpp in CMakePorts/libp7-baical are byte-identical to the Faramax/libp7-baical mirror (a 0-star fork of Mixaill/libp7-baical). The upstream site baical.net was not reachable; the CMakePorts port's last commit was 2020-02-06 (v5.2.0) while upstream may have newer releases. Claim words on the list ('high-speed', 'minimal CPU and memory') match the manual's speed chapter. [retier] First-party enqueue-only measurement with a flawed harness (ignores rejected calls, 64 MB pool, no delivery timed, whole-ms timer); baselines not like for like (vsprintf with 6 args vs one deferred integer). Abandoned port at v5.2.0; LGPL-3.0-or-later.
