name: uberlog
baseline: synchronous write-per-message file logging (a 'naive logging system' that issues one OS write call per message)
workload: README Benchmarks: time taken inside the calling program to format a roughly 200-byte message and push it into the shared-memory ring buffer (200 ns Windows, 280 ns Linux), against a hypothetical naive logger costing about 1500 ns for a 100-byte write() plus an assumed 1000 ns of formatting.
claimed_speedup: README: 200 ns (Windows) and 280 ns (Linux) per formatted message, 350 MB/s and 465 MB/s throughput, versus about 2500 ns per message for a naive write-per-message logger, 'a 10x speedup over a naive system'; at 100000 messages per second the naive logger spends 25% of time logging against 2% for uberlog. Ratios derived from page data: 2500/280 is about 8.9x on Linux and 2500/200 is 12.5x on Windows.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README numbers. The repo build script uses clang++ -O2 -ggdb -std=c++11 on Linux and macOS; an msvc/ project covers Windows.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700K (Windows and Linux)
tradeoffs: Multi-process design: a spawned child process (uberlogger) drains a shared-memory ring buffer and writes the file, so a crash in the main process still flushes earlier messages; the caller stalls only when the ring is full. Adds a second process and shared memory; fixed log line format unless you derive from Logger; printf-compatible type-safe formatting (tsf); log rolling built in; C++11.
caveats: The baseline is hypothetical, not a measured run: the 2500 ns figure adds a quoted ~1500 ns write() cost to an assumed 1000 ns of formatting. test.cpp does time a 5-byte write() (BenchFileWriteLatency, 200000 iterations) and the logger latency modes (raw, simple fmt, param fmt; 50000 messages after 100 warmup into a 32 MB ring sized never to stall), but no result file is stored and the README numbers name no compiler or flags. test.cpp also has a 'spd comparison' benchmark that only times 1M uberlog Info() calls and contains no spdlog code; there are no spdlog numbers anywhere in the repo. Third-party logging shootouts found (MuggleWei cc_log_benchmark) do not list uberlog. Latency counts only the in-program cost, not the writer process's work. README itself says a naive logger is fine below many thousands of messages per second, and the 2018 Meltdown/KPTI benefit is 'not measured'. The seed lead (from a C++ book) says it is not as fast as specialized low-latency loggers. No commits since 2020-04-08 (over 6 years); no releases. [retier] Enricher, security bug: the embedded tsf no-argument fast path checks len <= staticbuf_size + 1 and then copies len + 1 bytes, so a no-argument message of 157 or 158 characters on Linux (156 or 157 on Windows) with the date prefix writes up to 2 bytes past Log()'s 200-byte stack buffer. Harness mismatch: the README cites ~200-byte formatted messages, but test.cpp's latency bench uses ~108-114 bytes and reports the mean only; the throughput bench sends raw 200-byte LogRaw messages with no formatting; the write() bench uses 5-byte writes. Each formatted message makes a syscall(__NR_gettid) on Linux, which undercuts the README's few-syscalls argument. One mutex per Logger; producers sleep-spin when the ring is full; the writer's idle backoff grows to 1024 ms; no fsync; timestamps use the standard-time offset, one hour off during DST.

name: bpftime

claimed_speedup: README: up to 10x lower uprobe overhead than kernel uprobe/uretprobe. Generated benchmark table: uprobe 2561.57 ns kernel vs 190.02 ns userspace (13.48x); uretprobe 3019.45 ns vs 187.10 ns (16.14x); uprobe+uretprobe 3119.28 ns vs 191.63 ns (16.28x).
hardware: Intel Core Ultra 7 258V (4 cores, 4 threads), 15.07 GB RAM, Linux 6.11.0-24-generic (results generated 2025-04-30)
tradeoffs: Runs eBPF programs in userspace via LD_PRELOAD or a daemon, so it only sees processes it is injected into; no kernel-wide view; needs its own verifier (PREVAIL) or the kernel verifier; kernel baseline requires root and a recent kernel.

OSDI '25 paper (usenix.org) was not opened (egress blocked); its claims come from search snippets. Not a sampling profiler; it is an instrumentation runtime.

name: RetroWrite
workload: Binary-only AddressSanitizer (BASan) and AFL coverage instrumentation inserted by static rewriting of x86_64 and aarch64 Linux binaries, versus Valgrind memcheck, source-level ASan and QEMU-mode AFL on SPEC CPU2006 C benchmarks and fuzzing targets.
claimed_speedup: IEEE S&P 2020 abstract (via search snippets): binary-only ASan 3x faster than Valgrind memcheck on SPEC CPU2006 C benchmarks while detecting 80% more bugs; AFL coverage instrumentation as fast as compiler instrumentation and 4.5x faster than QEMU-mode AFL; fuzzing throughput 4.2x (real-world) and 5.6x (LAVA-M) over QEMU AFL.
tradeoffs: Works only on position-independent (PIE) x86_64 and aarch64 Linux binaries with symbolization limits; the tool itself is Python but its output is ordinary assembler, so result binaries are usable from C++ workflows.
caveats: Numbers are from abstract snippets only; the paper (nebelwelt.net/files/20Oakland.pdf, hexhive.epfl.ch) is blocked by egress and the README makes only a qualitative zero-overhead claim, so CPU, compiler and per-benchmark numbers were not checked. Retier candidate to B once the paper is reachable. The tool is written in Python, but its output is instrumented x86_64/aarch64 binaries. x64 rewriting needs PIC/PIE binaries; aarch64 uses a different algorithm (thesis). Last commit 2025-04-26. [retier] Enricher: the 3x is against Valgrind memcheck, which checks different things (it also tracks uninitialised values), so it is not a like-for-like sanitizer comparison; the abstract snippet puts BASan about 0.65x slower than source-level ASan on SPEC2006 C, and a Purdue thesis snippet gives 7.5x for AFL over QEMU where the abstract says 4.5x. The x64 BASan pass skips memory operands that are not 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes, so 16-byte SSE/AVX accesses go unchecked, and it adds stack redzones only to functions that load a stack canary. Open issue #49: BASan-rewritten SPEC2006 gcc and bzip2 segfault on x64, with no maintainer reply. 29 open issues, last commit 2025-04-26.

name: AFL (american fuzzy lop)
baseline: blind fuzzing (random mutation without coverage guidance)
workload: Coverage reached on GNU patch 2.7.3 compiled with -O3, seeded with a dummy text file, one pass over the afl-fuzz input queue, AFL's coverage-guided model against blind fuzzing and against block-only and edge-only guidance; a second experiment with only deterministic stages seeded with a valid unified diff.
claimed_speedup: Coverage, not speed: AFL model reached 1,765 blocks and 2,597 edges versus 182 blocks / 205 edges (blind fuzzing S, single round), 228 / 265 (blind fuzzing L, comparable number of cycles), 855 / 1,130 (block-coverage guidance) and 1,452 / 2,070 (edge-coverage guidance), from an initial file at 156 / 163. Deterministic-only experiment seeded with a valid unified diff (initial 624 / 717): AFL model 1,452 blocks / 2,040 edges and 1 unique crash versus blind fuzzing 1,101 / 1,409, block coverage 1,255 / 1,649 and edge coverage 1,259 / 1,734, all with 0 crashes. Separate speed claims in the same docs: LLVM-mode instrumentation lets some slow CPU-bound programs run up to around 2x faster and stays within about 10% for fast binaries (versus afl-gcc/afl-clang assembly-level rewriting); the fork server usually gives 1.5x-2x on fast targets; deferred fork server 10x+ on some targets. The README calls the fuzzer far superior to blind fuzzing or coverage-only tools.

tradeoffs: Needs an instrumented target (afl-gcc, afl-clang or the LLVM plugin; QEMU mode for black-box binaries is about 2-5x slower than compile-time instrumentation) and takes input as a file; persistent and deferred modes need small code changes and care to reset state. caveats: First-party table in the project's own technical notes, one target and one session, no CPU, no run count and no repeat variance, so not reproducible as written. It measures discovered blocks and edges, not execs per second or time to bug, and the blind baseline is AFL's own fuzzer with guidance removed, not an independent blind fuzzer. The docs do not claim to beat libFuzzer: llvm_mode/README.llvm says the persistent mode is not as fast as pure in-process fuzzing such as LLVM's LibFuzzer, though much faster than the fork() model and more robust. name: cpp-lazy
baseline: std::ranges / std::views (libstdc++ 13): filter, chunk, chunk_by, lazy_split, stride, slide, zip, cartesian_product, repeat, take, join
workload: Google Benchmark (v1.9.1) microbenchmarks over 32-element std::arrays and a 32-character string: each timed iteration constructs the lz:: or std::views adaptor and walks it once with benchmark::DoNotOptimize on each element; the chart divides that time by 32. Built as C++23 with gcc 13.3.0.
claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks section plus bench/benchmarks-iterators-23.png, per-element column (lz vs std, i.e. time per 32-element pass divided by 32): filter 0.2263 ns vs 0.8116 ns (about 3.6x faster, derived from page data); chunks 0.2425 ns vs 0.6376 ns (about 2.6x); split_single (lz::split vs views::lazy_split on ' ') 0.3902 ns vs 0.5568 ns (about 1.4x); chunk_if 0.4922 ns vs 0.5351 ns (about 1.09x); flatten 0.7095 ns vs 0.7771 ns (about 1.10x). The split_multiple row (0.4866 ns vs 0.8532 ns) is not like-for-like: the std side passes the literal "o " to views::lazy_split, whose pattern then includes the terminating NUL and never matches (one piece instead of six), so it is excluded. Parity within about 1 to 4 percent: map 0.2384 vs 0.2374, repeat 0.2389 vs 0.2372, take_iterable 0.2397 vs 0.2378, take_iterator 0.2389 vs 0.2386, common 0.2399 vs 0.2386, pairwise 0.4477 vs 0.4602, zip2/zip3/zip4 0.4904/0.7233/0.9545 vs 0.4764/0.7238/0.9582, cartesian_product 1.1439 vs 1.1684. Slower than std: take_every 0.9186 ns vs 0.5455 ns for std::views::stride (about 1.7x slower).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3.0 (README); bench/CMakeLists.txt sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE or optimization flags and takes the standard from CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD (23 per the image name; views::chunk, chunk_by and stride need it), so the flags used are not public.
tradeoffs: Works in C++11 through C++23 (the std views need C++20/23), so it fills the gap for older standards; lz iterables hold references to non-view inputs (maybe_owned) unless copied; sentinel-based ranges need workarounds before C++17; API differs from std::ranges (lz::filter(...), not views::filter) and the library is far smaller than range-v3.
caveats: First-party benchmark with public code but no CPU model, no published optimization flags (bench/CMakeLists.txt sets none) and the standard library only implied (libstdc++ inferred from gcc 13.3.0), so tier C. Tiny workload: 32 elements; the filter predicate (i == 0) matches only the first element, so the 3.6x filter figure measures scanning 32 ints for one match. The README says iterable creation is excluded, but bench/benchmarks-iterators.cpp constructs both the lz and std views inside the timed loop. The split_multiple row is invalid as a comparison: std::views::lazy_split(to_split, "o ") treats the NUL terminator as part of the pattern and yields one piece while lz::split yields six (checked with g++ 13.3 -std=c++23: 1 vs 6 pieces); split_single uses a char delimiter and is like-for-like. take_every and cartesian_product iterate uninitialized arrays. Most other rows are at parity, and std::views::stride beats lz::take_every by 1.7x. Results come from a single PNG with no run-to-run variance and no comparison against range-v3. The repo was formerly MarcDirven/cpp-lazy (the lead URL) and now lives at Kaaserne/cpp-lazy. The lead's suggested category (filesystems-and-io) does not fit; this is a ranges/iterator library, filed under the new category ranges-and-views for the orchestrator to remap.

name: libsrt (srt_vector sort)
baseline: std::sort (GNU/Clang std::vector sort) and C qsort()
workload: examples/bench.cpp (now test/bench.cc): push 1,000,000 elements in ascending (or reversed) order into an srt_vector or std::vector, call sv_sort or std::sort 10 times (9 of the 10 calls sort already-sorted data), cleanup; whole sequence timed. Also 100 elements sorted 10,000 times. 8-bit values wrap to a 256-value sawtooth. No random input is ever timed.
claimed_speedup: Current README (no numbers): 8-bit elements by counting sort 'up to 5x faster than GNU/Clang std::vector sort (C++)'; 16/32/64-bit elements by MSD binary radix sort '2x-3x faster than GNU/Clang qsort() (C), performing similar to GNU/Clang std::vector sort (C++)'. The author's 2017 tables (doc/benchmarks.md at commit e678325, 64-bit g++ 5.2.1, i5-3330, 1M elements inserted in ascending order then sorted 10 times, insert and cleanup included): libsrt_vector_i8 0.027646 s vs cxx_vector_i8 (std::sort) 0.137919 s, about 5.0x; u8 0.026851 vs 0.150012 s, about 5.6x; i16 0.145145 vs 0.145665 s, 1.0x; u16 0.132487 vs 0.171347 s, 1.29x; i32 0.183137 vs 0.150832 s, libsrt about 0.82x (slower); u32 0.90x; i64 and u64 0.85x (slower); 32-byte generic elements via qsort 1.265519 vs 2.052374 s, 1.62x; reverse-order input gives the same pattern; 100 elements sorted 10000 times: u8 1.85x, i8 1.15x, 16/32/64-bit libsrt 0.65x-0.83x (slower). Ratios derived from page data. No qsort() timings are published, so the 2x-3x versus qsort() has no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 5.2.1 on Ubuntu 15.10 x86_64 (64-bit build); the doc only says the bench executable is built with 'make', which at commit e678325 means Makefile.inc defaults -pipe -O2 -fomit-frame-pointer (flags inferred from the public Makefile, not stated on the page).
hardware: Intel Core i5-3330 @3GHz, 6MB L3 (sort tables exist only for the 64-bit x86_64 run; the 32-bit and Allwinner A64 runs have no sort tables).
tradeoffs: C library with its own string, vector, bitset, set, map and hash map types; vector sort is only specialised for 8, 16, 32 and 64-bit element types, generic elements fall back to qsort(); concurrent read/write needs user locking; maps keep nodes in one linear block with index links; deletion is slower than insertion.
caveats: First-party only. The README claim has no numbers; the only timings are 2017 tables (doc/benchmarks.md at commit e678325) that the author removed from the doc in January 2018 and never re-ran on the current code. Those tables support the 8-bit counting-sort claim (about 5x on i8, 5.6x on u8 against libstdc++ std::sort, an O(n) counting sort against a comparison sort), but contradict 'performing similar to std::vector sort' for 32/64-bit: libsrt was 10-18% slower there, and 16/32/64-bit was 17-35% slower on 100-element vectors. The benchmark only sorts ascending or reversed input and re-sorts already-sorted data 9 times, and the time includes insertion and cleanup. Correctness bug: the 3-element and 4-element sorting networks used by the 16/32/64-bit MSD radix sort in src/saux/ssort.c are wrong at HEAD. BUILD_SORT3 leaves [1,3,2] unchanged, BUILD_SORT4 turns [3,4,1,2] into [1,3,2,4], and sv_sort on the i32 vector [1,3,2,8,9,10,11,12] returns it unsorted (hand trace). A Python port of the HEAD algorithm misplaces 114,854 of 1,000,000 random 32-bit values, while ascending, reversed and evens-then-odds inputs (the only ones the bench and stest.c use) come out sorted. This was checked on a port, not the compiled C. The 2017 code that produced the tables had a different BUILD_SORT4 that swaps b[0]/b[3] and b[1]/b[4], reading past a 4-element block. 8-bit counting sort is correct. Generic elements fall back to qsort(). Lead URL faragon.github.io/libsrt.html is API docs only (checked via the faragon/faragon.github.io repo). Filed under sorting; the project is a general C data-structure and string library. [retier] 8-bit counting sort about 5.0-5.6x vs libstdc++ std::sort (2017 tables, g++ 5.2.1, i5-3330, -O2); 32/64-bit libsrt sorts 0.82-0.90x and incorrect (s_msb stops one shift short; SORT3/SORT4 networks wrong); bench and stest use only ascending, reversed or evens-then-odds input; ssort.c untouched since 2019; no upstream issue filed.

name: Thrust (thrust::sort)
workload: CIS 565 student project sorts int arrays of 1,048,576 to 16,777,216 elements (values in [0,1000) or full int range) with std::sort on the CPU and thrust::sort on a Tesla T4, host/device transfers excluded.
claimed_speedup: thrust::sort vs std::sort on int arrays, medians of 7 runs after a warm-up in ms (perf/data/sort.csv column median_ms; README sort table): 1,048,576 elements in [0,1000): 0.67 vs 54.6 ms (about 81x, derived from page data); 16,777,216 in [0,1000): 3.73 vs 912.7 ms (about 245x, derived from page data); 1,048,576 any int: 0.90 vs 88.8 ms (about 99x, derived from page data); 8,388,608 any int: 2.52 vs 801.6 ms (about 318x, derived from page data). GPU (Tesla T4) vs one CPU thread, host/device transfers excluded.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (the project's CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release), CUDA 13.3, driver 610.57, Ubuntu 22.04.5; host compiler and its flags not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.30GHz (4 vCPUs, Google Cloud VM), NVIDIA Tesla T4 16 GB
license: Apache-2.0 (Thrust, with portions under BSL-1.0 and a FreeBSD-derived licence); CUB, which supplies thrust::sort's CUDA radix sort, is BSD-3-Clause; libcu++ is Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception
tradeoffs: Requires a CUDA GPU for the speedups (Thrust also has TBB, OpenMP and serial CPU backends, but the benchmark measured the CUDA backend). Header-only; device memory and transfer costs are not included in the sorted time; CUDA backend uses CUB radix sort for primitive keys with the default comparator and falls back to merge sort otherwise.
caveats: This compares a GPU radix sort (Thrust dispatching to CUB) with single-threaded std::sort on one vCPU, so it measures GPU vs one CPU core and excludes host/device transfers (std::copy and device_vector construction sit outside the timers); it is not a library-to-library win. The thrust::sort timing includes CUB's per-call temporary-storage cudaMalloc/cudaFree. The evidence is a student project README (Josh0323/Project2-Stream-Compaction, fork of the course template, 0 stars, no licence; one machine, host compiler and standard library not stated, CPU model only 'Xeon @ 2.30GHz', 16M full-range run missing because of a VM restart), so tier C. The Thrust project README and NVIDIA/cccl contain no performance numbers; a vendor claim that thrust::sort is '5x to 100x faster than STL and TBB' was seen only as a search-result snippet and is not used. Thrust development moved into NVIDIA/cccl (standalone NVIDIA/thrust archived 2024-03-21); last_commit and star counts for the live repo are from NVIDIA/cccl. Category changed from the guessed thread-pools-work-stealing because the only numeric comparison is a sort.

baseline: libcoro thread_pool (jbaldwin/libcoro), with HPX as a second weaker baseline

name: Intel Parallel STL
workload: Sum of a 1 GiB array of 268435456 floats, all set to 1.0f, using std::reduce(std::execution::par, first, last, T(0), std::plus<T>) versus serial std::accumulate, both from GCC 12's libstdc++. libstdc++'s <execution> uses its bundled Parallel STL with the oneTBB backend. The f64 rows accumulate the same float array into a double. Google Benchmark with MinTime 10 s and UseRealTime; the error is checked against the expected sum.
claimed_speedup: AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl: std::reduce<par>/f32 1950894 ns (550.384 GB/s) versus std::accumulate/f32 192162701 ns (5.58767 GB/s), about 98x (derived from page data); f64 1959062 ns versus 192266754 ns, about 98x (derived from page data). AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl: std::reduce<par, f32> 2913596 ns versus std::accumulate<f32> 219734340 ns, about 75x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (stated in the README for the Graviton4 and Zen4 runs). CMake Release build: CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE becomes '-O3 -DNDEBUG -O2', and the last -O wins, so the build is -O2. For GNU compilers CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS to CMAKE_GCC_FLAGS ('-march=native -fopenmp'), so those flags do apply; tags v0.1.0, v0.2.0, v0.3.0, v0.4.0, v0.5.3 and HEAD v0.7.2 all use the same logic. oneTBB is fetched from uxlfoundation/oneTBB branch master (unpinned), and USE_INTEL_TBB defaults to ON on Linux without CUDA. Google Benchmark v1.9.1.
hardware: AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl (Google Benchmark reports 96 x 2000 MHz; single NUMA node) for the headline row. AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl (192 x 3701.95 MHz reported; dual-socket per the README's observation; exact CPU SKU not stated) for the second row.
stars_or_usage: 777 stars and 122 forks on uxlfoundation/oneDPL, which github.com/intel/parallelstl now serves. Intel contributed its Parallel STL to GCC 9's libstdc++ as the implementation of the C++17 parallel algorithms (Phoronix 'GCC 9 libstdc++ Lands The C++17 Parallel Algorithms Implementation From Intel' and the gcc.gnu.org libstdc++ RFC of November 2017; WebSearch snippets only).
tradeoffs: Parallel backend needs oneTBB at link time. The standalone intel/parallelstl repository now serves the oneDPL repository (oneAPI DPC++ Library, Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions), which targets SYCL devices and needs the oneAPI toolchain for the device parts.
caveats: Indirect evidence: the benchmark runs libstdc++'s bundled <execution> implementation (a vendored copy of Intel's Parallel STL as contributed to GCC 9, backed by oneTBB). It does not build intel/parallelstl or oneDPL, and oneDPL's oneapi::dpl::execution policies were not measured. The baseline is a serial std::accumulate, whose strict left fold makes it latency-bound on the floating-point add chain, not memory-bound. On Graviton4 the single-thread unrolled/f32 loop (38034000 ns) is already 5.05x faster than std::accumulate/f32 (derived from page data), so 96-core parallelism accounts for only about 19.5x of the 98x (derived from page data). A std::reduce(seq) or unrolled serial baseline would show a far smaller gain. On Graviton4, hand-written OpenMP (neon/f32/openmp 1901684 ns) and fork_union (neon/f32/av::fork_union 1890173 ns; serial/f32/av::fork_union 1889686 ns) match or beat std::reduce<par>/f32 at 1950894 ns. The Graviton4 rows report 550 to 568 GB/s, above the 537.6 GB/s theoretical DRAM peak of one Graviton4 socket (12 channels of DDR5-5600; WikiChip and The Next Platform, snippet only). Repeated iterations over the 1 GiB buffer are therefore partly served from the 96 x 2 MB L2 and 36 MB L3, and absolute bandwidth is slightly inflated. std::accumulate<f32> shows 93.75 percent error because a float accumulator stops growing at 2^24; the f64 row is accurate. The README tables are single hand-pasted runs with no variance reported. oneTBB master is not pinned, and fork_union is fetched from its main branch. The benchmark repository has no LICENSE file. The DGX-H100 rows were not used: CUDA machines default USE_INTEL_TBB to OFF, so the backend is unclear, and that table's std::reduce<par, f64> and <par_unseq, f64> rows show error,%=100 (wrong result). The Zen4 table dates from the May 2024 README refresh and uses older row labels. The Graviton4 table was added in May 2025 and its std::reduce labels match the current reduce_bench.cpp. No comparison against MSVC STL, libc++ parallel algorithms or GNU parallel mode.

name: NVthreads
baseline: Atlas (HP persistent-memory failure-atomic-section library) and Mnemosyne (word-level STM persistent memory); plain pthreads is faster than NVthreads
workload: Making multi-threaded programs durable on emulated NVM (modified tmpfs on DRAM adding a 1,000 ns delay to each 4 KB page write): 14 Phoenix and PARSEC benchmarks with 12 threads against pthreads, DThreads and Atlas (Atlas could not run canneal or dedup); a microbenchmark that allocates 1000 pages (4 MB) and has 4 threads modify a random fraction (5%-100%) of each page, against Atlas and Mnemosyne; PageRank on the Slashdot graph (82K vertices, 950K edges) against Atlas and Mnemosyne, and on the 1.2 GB LiveJournal graph against Atlas only (Mnemosyne could not run it).
claimed_speedup: EuroSys 2017 paper: 'NVthreads is 2x-10x faster than Mnemosyne and more than 2x faster than Atlas'; 'in 10 out of the 12 workloads on which Atlas ran, NVthreads is from 7% to 100x faster depending upon the workload' (about 7% and 50% slower than Atlas on streamcluster and reverse index); microbenchmark 'NVthreads is 3x-30x faster than these systems' (Mnemosyne and Atlas 70x to over 200x slower than pthreads, NVthreads 25x down to 5x slower). PageRank on the Slashdot graph at 12 cores: 170 ms per iteration vs 500 ms Atlas (about 2.9x, derived from page data) and 5 s Mnemosyne (about 29x, derived from page data; the paper's prose says '10x faster than Mnemosyne'); LiveJournal: 5 s vs 29 s for Atlas, 'almost 6x faster', while the pthreads version takes under 1 s per iteration. Against plain pthreads NVthreads is slower: 9 of 14 apps under 28% overhead, but reverse index (5.5x), canneal (4.1x), dedup (6.7x) and ferret (4.8x) are over 4x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper; the library's src/Makefile builds with g++ -g -m64 -msse2 -O3 -DNDEBUG -shared -fPIC -DLOCK_OWNERSHIP -DDETERM_MEMORY_ALLOC (compiler version unstated).
hardware: Two Intel Xeon X5650 (12 cores at 2.67 GHz), 198 GB RAM, 600 GB SSD, Ubuntu 14.04 (Linux 3.16.7); NVM emulated with a modified tmpfs on DRAM adding 1000 ns per 4 KB page write
tradeoffs: Drop-in pthreads replacement that adds persistence: Dthreads-style multi-process execution with copy-on-write page buffering, page-granularity redo logs and recovery; overhead versus plain pthreads is 20 to 28% on easy workloads and over 4x on others; needs an NVM filesystem; research prototype ('use at your own risk'); log space 165 MB to 300 MB versus 550 MB-3.2 GB for Mnemosyne in the microbenchmark.
caveats: The baselines are other research persistence systems (Atlas, Mnemosyne), not std::thread or pthreads; NVthreads is slower than unmodified pthreads (over 4x on four PARSEC/Phoenix apps, about 5x on LiveJournal PageRank), so it is not faster than the category incumbent. NVM is emulated with software delays; Atlas could not run canneal and dedup, Mnemosyne ran only the microbenchmark and the small Slashdot PageRank graph (it crashes above 4 MB of durable data), and Mnemosyne's constant 2 s fork/pmalloc overhead was excluded. The paper's prose ratio for Mnemosyne on Slashdot (10x) does not match its own 170 ms vs 5 s figures (about 29x). Compiler flags for the benchmark applications are not stated in the paper. The root COPYING is GPL-2.0 (copyleft for a drop-in pthreads replacement) while the awesome-cpp listing says LGPL-2.1, and third-parties/ vendors Atlas, Mnemosyne and DThreads under their own licenses. The README calls it a research prototype under development, not for production. Category thread-pools-work-stealing is the closest wave-11 fit; the project is really persistent-memory threading.

name: Rayon
baseline: OpenMP parallel for (C++ with static and dynamic scheduling)

Rayon static is par_chunks_mut with one stripe per worker in N-body and plain par_iter_mut (Rayon's default adaptive splitting) in connected components; Rayon dynamic is par_iter_mut().with_max_len(1). OpenMP uses schedule(static) and schedule(dynamic, 1).

tradeoffs: Rust-only (C++ projects must call it over FFI or rewrite the loop); par_iter is a one-line change and the API guarantees data-race freedom; dynamic splitting by default means no static schedule, so uniform loops pay stealing overhead and tiny per-item work can run slower than serial (forum reports, not opened).
caveats: Evidence is a side result of a competing library's benchmark: the README belongs to Fork Union (ForkUnion, Rust and C++), whose author promotes it as about 3-6x faster than OpenMP and 12-16x faster than Rayon, so the figures were not produced by the Rayon project. Rayon beats OpenMP only in a minority of cells; OpenMP's 'dynamic' columns use schedule(dynamic, 1), a one-vertex grain whose shared queue collapses at high thread counts (0.1-0.4 GTEPS, as the README itself explains), which is why the 15-50x Rayon wins appear; against OpenMP's static schedule Rayon is behind on most machines (up to 6.4x lower GTEPS on Graviton 5, derived from page data) and it also loses dynamic connected components on the M5 Pro. The one N-body win is on the Windows box where the README names MinGW-GCC, so the OpenMP runtime there is probably libgomp, not libomp. Fork Union's documentation disagrees on fast-math: the scripts/nbody.cpp and nbody.rs headers say the C++ build adds -ffast-math, while scripts/CMakeLists.txt says strict IEEE math is deliberate and adds only -ffp-contract=off; which build produced the tables is not stated. Rayon 'static' in connected components is plain par_iter_mut with adaptive splitting, not a fixed per-worker stripe as the doc comment says. Exact CPU models and compiler versions are not given, and the benchmark does not use the cited 'oneTBB parallel_for' or 'std::execution::par' baselines. Rayon's own repo has no comparison against OpenMP, TBB or std::execution::par: the README carries no numbers, PR #1156 (par_sort sync) says 'mostly the same or slightly better' with no figures, and rayon-demo prints sequential-vs-parallel speedups at run time without stored results. A search snippet (arXiv 2502.15536, NPB-Rust, page blocked and not opened) reports Rayon slower than C++ OpenMP on the NAS kernels; snippet only. [retier] Enricher: Fork Union's scripts/nbody.rs and propagation.rs call pool.install from the main thread, which is not a pool worker, on every round (twice per N-body iteration), taking the in_worker_cold path (global injector push plus a Mutex/Condvar LockLatch wait), while OpenMP's master thread joins the work; one install around the whole loop or use_current_thread is the idiomatic form. N-body OpenMP is pinned (OMP_PROC_BIND=spread) and the Rayon pool is not. So the Rayon numbers are pessimistic and its wins are not inflated. Minimum toolchain: published 1.12.0 declares rust_version 1.80; main's Cargo.toml says rustc 1.85, edition 2024. Gotchas: Mutex/OnceLock reentrancy deadlock (#592 open, #1251), slowdown with non-power-of-two thread counts (#968 open), quadratic stealing cost (#394 open), spawn panics abort without a panic_handler, 32 yield rounds before sleeping.

name: Lace (trolando)
baseline: Intel TBB, Cilk Plus (Cilk++), OpenMP and Wool (Wool is the parity target, not a claimed loss)
workload: Fine-grained fork-join benchmarks (fib, UTS, N-Queens, matmul, strassen, cilksort and others from the Cilk-5 suite) timed on multi-core machines; the exact paper table was not seen.
claimed_speedup: No numbers seen. Paper abstract (search snippet): the split deque and the private-deque variant implemented in Lace have 'similar low overhead and high scalability as Wool', i.e. parity with Wool, not faster. Third-party 2020 University of Twente thesis (search snippet): on Unbalanced Tree Search, Fibonacci and Strassen, Lace performs best, CilkPlus and TBB intermediate, OpenMP worst by far; no figures seen.

Builds on Linux, macOS, Windows (MSVC, MinGW) and FreeBSD.

name: Spice
workload: Binary tree summation fork-join (100M nodes) at up to 16 threads, and a 1000-node small tree, versus a Zig sequential baseline and Rayon on the same algorithm.
claimed_speedup: 100M-node tree sum (bench/README.md SVGs): Zig sequential baseline 3.63 ns/node, Spice 3.93 ns at 1 thread (sub-ns overhead), 0.36 ns at 16 threads (~11x); Rust sequential baseline 7.48 ns/node, Rayon 22.99 ns at 1 thread (~15 ns overhead), 1.64 ns at 16 threads (~14x). Spice at 16 threads is ~4.6x faster than Rayon in absolute per-node time (derived from page data), but the languages' baselines differ 2x. 1000-node tree: Rayon becomes ~60x slower than its baseline at 32 threads on 16 vCPUs, while Spice stays flat because no work is distributed.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.14.0-dev.564+75cf7fca9, ReleaseFast; Rayon side rustc 1.77.2 / cargo 1.77.1 with Criterion
hardware: Google Cloud c4-standard-16 (16 vCPUs, 60 GB), europe-west4, NixOS 24.05, Linux 6.6.41; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Heartbeat scheduling (work shared every ~100 us), fork/join only, Zig API.
caveats: Cross-language comparison: the Zig sequential baseline (3.63 ns/node) is twice as fast as the Rust one (7.48 ns/node), so absolute Spice-vs-Rayon times mix scheduler and codegen differences; the author compares each against its own language's baseline. Rayon scales better (14x vs 11x at 16 threads); Spice's win is sub-nanosecond fork/join overhead and no slowdown on tiny inputs. Single workload (tree sum), single run of make bench, August 2024. Author calls it a research project with minimal tests. Zig, usable from C++ only via a C ABI wrapper.

name: FastThreadPool (komrad36)
baseline: None named by the author; std::async, boost::asio::thread_pool and BS::thread_pool are the natural incumbents (inferred by the search agent, never compared)
workload: None: the repository contains no benchmark code and reports no measurement.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'A super fast lock-free (though not always wait-free) thread pool.'
tradeoffs: fast_thread_pool.h (183 lines, header-only) is a lock-free multi-producer multi-consumer linked-list queue of plain function pointers (void (*)()), not a full pool: no worker threads are created by the class, no arguments or return values (no std::function, no futures), one heap allocation per AddWork. Waiters spin with _mm_pause; the README itself says it should sleep instead of spin after a while (TODO) and could be faster with block queues, so idle consumers burn CPU.
caveats: Pure assertion with no numbers and no baseline run; kept as a tier D record only because the author (komrad36) is a known performance-oriented developer. The repo has 5 commits, all on 2021-10-18 and 2021-10-19, no tests and no benchmark. Despite the name, fast_thread_pool.h (183 lines) is not a thread pool: it is an intrusive linked-list MPMC queue of plain void(*)() function pointers with AddWork/RemoveWork; it creates no threads and has no worker loop, futures, arguments or captures, so users must write the workers themselves. AddWork and RemoveWork spin with _mm_pause on a tag bit set in the head/tail pointers, which acts as a short spinlock, so a preempted thread can stall the others (not lock-free in the formal sense despite the README). Every AddWork heap-allocates a node with new and every RemoveWork deletes one. The README's own TODOs say it 'could probably be faster with block queues' and should sleep instead of spinning when idle. The memory-order annotations (S1-S9, L1-L6) are not backed by a proof or test; L4 reads the tail with a relaxed load before reading pHead->m_next with acquire, which looked unproven on weakly ordered CPUs (not analysed further). Not comparable to std::async or BS::thread_pool in features, so any speed claim would need a like-for-like queue benchmark. [retier] Enricher (code reading): relaxed tail read followed by pHead->m_next lets a consumer on ARM or POWER see a null next pointer and strand all queued items; Pause() is a no-op on MSVC; not lock-free (tag bits spin).
